title: LA BELLE AU BOIS DORMANT
titleEn: The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood
work: Histoires ou contes du temps passé
part: The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood
source: Charles Perrault, « LA BELLE AU BOIS DORMANT », dans Histoires ou contes du temps passé. Avec des Moralitez (Paris, Claude Barbin, 1697) ; texte de l’édition originale d’après la transcription de Wikisource, orthographe de 1697 conservée. Prononciation : français standard moderne ; les graphies de 1697 sont lues selon l’usage moderne.
about: Perrault’s tale does not stop where most later retellings do: after the hundred years’ sleep and the waking, the Princess marries her Prince in secret and bears him two children, and the 1697 story goes on to his mother, an Ogress by birth, who orders the children and then their mother served up at her table. The telling is a courtier’s, dry and knowing, full of the offices and customs of a great household of Perrault’s own day, which the notes explain as they arise. It closes with a verse moral on the merits of waiting for a husband, and a teasing doubt that any woman would care to wait so long.

sentences.t: Il estoit une fois un Roi & une Reine qui estoient si faschez de n’avoir point d’enfans, si faschez qu’on ne sçauroit dire.
sentences.say: Il était une fois un Roi et une Reine qui étaient si fâchés de n’avoir point d’enfants, si fâchés qu’on ne saurait dire.
sentences.l: There was one time a King and a Queen who were so grieved at not having any children, so grieved that one could not say.
sentences.i: Once upon a time there was a King and a Queen who were so sorrowful at having no children, so sorrowful that there are no words for it.
sentences.n: «Il estoit une fois» is the storyteller’s fixed opening: «il» is the impersonal ‘it’, standing where English says ‘there’, «estoit» is the 1697 spelling of «était» ‘was’, and «une fois» is ‘one time, once’. Lectorium gives it the matching English formula, ‘once upon a time’, in every tale it opens (Cendrillon prints it «Il eſtoit», with the long s). «estoient» is likewise «étaient» ‘were’, and «faschez» is «fâchés»: in 1697 «fâché» meant ‘grieved, sorely distressed’, a sadder word than modern «fâché» ‘annoyed, cross’. «ne … point» is a firm ‘not’, and «enfans» is «enfants». «qu’on ne sçauroit dire» is ‘more than one could say’: «sçauroit», the old spelling of «saurait», is the conditional of «sçavoir» (modern «savoir») ‘to know how’, used with «ne» for ‘could not’. «&» is the printer’s sign for «et» ‘and’.

sentences.t: Ils allerent à toutes les eaux du monde : vœux, pelerinages, menuës devotions, tout fut mis en œuvre, & rien n’y faisoit.
sentences.say: Ils allèrent à toutes les eaux du monde : vœux, pèlerinages, menues dévotions, tout fut mis en œuvre, et rien n’y faisait.
sentences.l: They went to all the waters of the world: vows, pilgrimages, small devotions, everything was put to work, and nothing did any good.
sentences.i: They went to take the waters at every spring in the world; vows, pilgrimages, little devotions, everything was tried, and nothing helped.
sentences.n: «allerent» (modern «allèrent») ‘went’ is the passé simple, the tense in which French tells a story: each verb in it is an event, done and finished. It has left everyday speech, where the passé composé («ils sont allés») took its place, and English renders it with its plain past. «tout fut mis en œuvre» ‘everything was put to work’ is its passive. «les eaux» are healing springs, where the well-to-do went for cures, including cures for childlessness. «menuës devotions» (modern «menues dévotions») are small acts of piety. «rien n’y faisoit» is ‘nothing made any difference to it’; its imperfect says that failure followed failure.

sentences.t: Enfin, pourtant, la Reine devint grosse, & accoucha d’une fille ; on fit un beau Baptesme ;
sentences.say: Enfin, pourtant, la Reine devint grosse, et accoucha d’une fille ; on fit un beau Baptême ;
sentences.l: At last, however, the Queen became big [with child], and was delivered of a daughter; they held a fine Christening;
sentences.i: At last, however, the Queen found herself with child and gave birth to a daughter; there was a splendid christening;
sentences.n: «devint grosse» ‘became big’ was the plain word of the time for ‘became pregnant’, and the literal line supplies ‘with child’ in brackets; «accoucher de» is ‘to give birth to’. «devint», «accoucha» and «fit» are passé simple. «on fit» ‘one made’ is ‘they held’. «Baptesme» is the 1697 spelling of «baptême», an «s» before a consonant where modern French puts a circumflex.

sentences.t: on donna pour Maraines à la petite Princesse toutes les Fées qu’on pust trouver dans le Païs (il s’en trouva sept), afin que, chacune d’elles luy faisant un don, comme c’estoit la coustume des Fées en ce temps-là, la Princesse eust, par ce moyen, toutes les perfections imaginables.
sentences.say: on donna pour Marraines à la petite Princesse toutes les Fées qu’on pût trouver dans le Pays (il s’en trouva sept), afin que, chacune d’elles lui faisant un don, comme c’était la coutume des Fées en ce temps-là, la Princesse eût, par ce moyen, toutes les perfections imaginables.
sentences.l: they gave as godmothers to the little Princess all the fairies that one could find in the Country (there were found seven of them), so that, each of them making her a gift, as it was the custom of the fairies in that time, the Princess might have, by this means, all the perfections imaginable.
sentences.i: for godmothers the little Princess was given all the fairies that could be found in the land (seven were found), so that each of them might bestow a gift on her, as was the fairies’ custom in those days, and by this means the Princess would have every perfection imaginable.
sentences.n: «Maraines» is the 1697 spelling of «marraines» ‘godmothers’, sponsors at the christening, from whom a gift for the child was expected. «Païs» is «pays» ‘country, land’, «coustume» is «coutume» ‘custom’, and «luy» is «lui» ‘to her’, with the 1697 «y». «il s’en trouva sept» is ‘there were found seven of them’, «en» standing for the fairies. «eust», the 1697 spelling of «eût», is the imperfect subjunctive of «avoir», required after «afin que» ‘so that’: a formal tense that modern speech avoids, rendered in English with ‘might’ or ‘would’. «pust» could be the same tense of «pouvoir» (modern «pût») or its passé simple (modern «put»); the sense is ‘could’ either way.

sentences.t: Aprés les ceremonies du Baptesme, toute la compagnie revint au Palais du Roi, où il y avoit un grand festin pour les Fées.
sentences.say: Après les cérémonies du Baptême, toute la compagnie revint au Palais du Roi, où il y avait un grand festin pour les Fées.
sentences.l: After the ceremonies of the Christening, all the company came back to the Palace of the King, where there was a great feast for the fairies.
sentences.i: When the christening ceremonies were over, the whole company returned to the King’s palace, where a great feast was laid on for the fairies.
sentences.n: «il y avoit» ‘there was’ is built on «avoir» ‘to have’, word for word ‘it there had’; «avoit» is the 1697 spelling of «avait». «Aprés» has an acute accent where modern «après» has a grave, and «revint» is the passé simple of «revenir» ‘to come back’.

sentences.t: On mit devant chacune d’elles un couvert magnifique, avec un estui d’or massif où il y avoit une cuillier, une fourchette, & un couteau de fin or, garnis de diamants & de rubis.
sentences.say: On mit devant chacune d’elles un couvert magnifique, avec un étui d’or massif où il y avait une cuillère, une fourchette, et un couteau de fin or, garnis de diamants et de rubis.
sentences.l: They set before each of them a magnificent place, with a case of solid gold in which there were a spoon, a fork, and a knife of fine gold, set with diamonds and rubies.
sentences.i: Before each of them was laid a magnificent place, with a case of solid gold holding a spoon, a fork and a knife of fine gold, all set with diamonds and rubies.
sentences.n: A «couvert» is a place laid at table, with its implements; the «estui» (modern «étui») is a fitted case to hold them. «cuillier» is an older spelling of «cuiller» ‘spoon’, and «garnis» ‘furnished, adorned’ agrees with all three pieces. «mit» is the passé simple of «mettre» ‘to put, to set’.

sentences.t: Mais, comme chacun prenoit sa place à table, on vit entrer une vieille Fée, qu’on n’avait point priée, parce qu’il y avait plus de cinquante ans qu’elle n’estoit sortie d’une Tour, & qu’on la croyoit morte ou enchantée.
sentences.say: Mais, comme chacun prenait sa place à table, on vit entrer une vieille Fée, qu’on n’avait point priée, parce qu’il y avait plus de cinquante ans qu’elle n’était sortie d’une Tour, et qu’on la croyait morte ou enchantée.
sentences.l: But, as each one was taking his place at table, they saw come in an old fairy, whom they had not invited, because it was more than fifty years that she had not come out of a Tower, and [because] they believed her dead or enchanted.
sentences.i: But as everyone was taking their places at table, in came an old fairy who had not been invited, because for more than fifty years she had not come out of a tower, and she was believed to be dead or under a spell.
sentences.n: «prier» here is ‘to invite’, an older sense beside ‘to pray, to beg’. «il y avait plus de cinquante ans qu’elle n’estoit sortie» is ‘it was more than fifty years that she had not gone out’, the French way of saying ‘for more than fifty years’, with «ne» alone as the negative, as often in such clauses. «& qu’on la croyoit» continues the «parce que», which the literal line repeats in brackets. The witness prints «avait» here, with the modern ending, beside «avoit» and «croyoit» elsewhere; the mixture stands in Lectorium’s witness, which it prints unaltered. «on vit entrer» ‘one saw come in’ is passé simple.

sentences.t: Le Roi lui fit donner un couvert ; mais il n’y eut pas moyen de lui donner un estuy d’or massif, comme aux autres, parce que l’on n’en avoit fait faire que sept pour les sept Fées.
sentences.say: Le Roi lui fit donner un couvert ; mais il n’y eut pas moyen de lui donner un étui d’or massif, comme aux autres, parce que l’on n’en avait fait faire que sept pour les sept Fées.
sentences.l: The King had her given a place; but there was no way to give her a case of solid gold, as to the others, because they had had only seven of them made for the seven fairies.
sentences.i: The King had a place laid for her, but there was no way of giving her a case of solid gold like the others, because only seven had been made, for the seven fairies.
sentences.n: «fit donner» and «avoit fait faire» are «faire» with an infinitive, ‘to have something done’: the King does not serve her himself, and the cases had been ordered to be made, word for word ‘made make’. «ne … que» is ‘not … but’, that is, ‘only’, and «en» is ‘of them’. «estuy» is the same word as «estui» two sentences back, spelled with «y», and «lui» here stands beside «luy» elsewhere: the book spells freely.

sentences.t: La vieille crût qu’on la méprisait, & grommela quelques menaces entre ses dents.
sentences.say: La vieille crut qu’on la méprisait, et grommela quelques menaces entre ses dents.
sentences.l: The old one believed that they despised her, and grumbled some threats between her teeth.
sentences.i: The old fairy thought she was being slighted, and muttered threats under her breath.
sentences.n: «la vieille» ‘the old one’ is the old fairy; French needs no noun after the adjective. «crût» is the passé simple of «croire» ‘to believe’, modern «crut»; the circumflex is the printer’s. «méprisait», printed with the modern ending, is ‘despised, held in contempt’: to her the lesser place is an insult. «grommeler entre ses dents» ‘to grumble between one’s teeth’ is ‘to mutter’.

sentences.t: Une des jeunes Fées qui se trouva auprés d’elle, l’entendit, et, jugeant qu’elle pourroit donner quelque fâcheux don à la petite princesse, alla dés qu’on fut sorti de table, se cacher derriere la tapisserie, afin de parler la derniere, & de pouvoir réparer, autant qu’il luy seroit possible, le mal que la vieille aurait fait.
sentences.say: Une des jeunes Fées qui se trouva auprès d’elle, l’entendit, et, jugeant qu’elle pourrait donner quelque fâcheux don à la petite princesse, alla dès qu’on fut sorti de table, se cacher derrière la tapisserie, afin de parler la dernière, et de pouvoir réparer, autant qu’il lui serait possible, le mal que la vieille aurait fait.
sentences.l: One of the young fairies, who happened to be near her, heard her, and, judging that she might give some grievous gift to the little princess, went, as soon as they had risen from table, to hide behind the tapestry, in order to speak the last, and to be able to repair, as far as it would be possible for her, the harm that the old one would have done.
sentences.i: One of the young fairies, who happened to be sitting beside her, overheard, and judging that she might give the little Princess some harmful gift, went as soon as they rose from table and hid behind the tapestry, so as to speak last and be able to undo, as far as lay in her power, whatever harm the old fairy might have done.
sentences.n: «se trouva auprés d’elle» ‘found herself near her’ is ‘happened to be beside her’; «auprés» and «dés» are 1697 for «auprès» and «dès» ‘as soon as’. «fâcheux» here is ‘unfortunate, harmful’, from the same «fâcher» as the King and Queen’s grief. Tapestries hung on the walls of great rooms, and one could stand hidden behind them. «pourroit», «seroit» and «aurait fait» are conditionals: what the fairy expects, seen from the past; the witness prints the last with the modern ending. «on fut sorti de table» ‘one was gone out from table’ is a past anterior.

sentences.t: Cependant les Fées commencerent à faire leurs dons à la Princesse.
sentences.say: Cependant les Fées commencèrent à faire leurs dons à la Princesse.
sentences.l: Meanwhile the fairies began to make their gifts to the Princess.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the fairies began to bestow their gifts on the Princess.
sentences.n: «Cependant» here is ‘meanwhile’, its older sense; today it more often means ‘however’. «commencerent» is the passé simple, modern «commencèrent», printed without the grave accent.

sentences.t: La plus jeune luy donna pour don qu’elle seroit la plus belle personne du monde, celle d’aprés qu’elle auroit de l’esprit comme un Ange, la troisiéme qu’elle auroit une grace admirable à tout ce qu’elle feroit ;
sentences.say: La plus jeune lui donna pour don qu’elle serait la plus belle personne du monde, celle d’après qu’elle aurait de l’esprit comme un Ange, la troisième qu’elle aurait une grâce admirable à tout ce qu’elle ferait ;
sentences.l: The youngest gave her as a gift that she would be the most beautiful person in the world, the one after, that she would have wit like an Angel, the third, that she would have an admirable grace in all that she would do;
sentences.i: The youngest gave her the gift of being the most beautiful person in the world; the next, that she would have the wit of an angel; the third, that she would have a wonderful grace in everything she did;
sentences.n: «donner pour don» ‘to give as a gift’ is the fairies’ formula, and after the first fairy it is simply understood. Each gift is a «que» clause with a verb in the conditional («seroit», «auroit», «feroit», 1697 for «serait», «aurait», «ferait»), the future as seen from the past. «esprit» is ‘wit’, quickness and grace of mind. «troisiéme» has the acute accent that modern «troisième» has changed to a grave.

sentences.t: la quatriéme qu’elle danseroit parfaitement bien, la cinquiéme qu’elle chanteroit comme un Rossignol, & la sixiéme, qu’elle joüeroit de toutes sortes d’instrumens dans la derniere perfection.
sentences.say: la quatrième qu’elle danserait parfaitement bien, la cinquième qu’elle chanterait comme un Rossignol, et la sixième, qu’elle jouerait de toutes sortes d’instruments dans la dernière perfection.
sentences.l: the fourth that she would dance perfectly well, the fifth that she would sing like a Nightingale, and the sixth, that she would play all sorts of instruments to the utmost perfection.
sentences.i: the fourth, that she would dance to perfection; the fifth, that she would sing like a nightingale; and the sixth, that she would play every kind of instrument with consummate skill.
sentences.n: «jouer de» is ‘to play’ an instrument, and «dans la derniere perfection» is ‘in the last perfection’: «dernier» ‘last’ in the sense of ‘highest degree’. The six gifts are the accomplishments admired in a princess at court: beauty, wit, grace, dancing, singing and music. «joüeroit» and «instrumens» are 1697 spellings of «jouerait» and «instruments».

sentences.t: Le rang de la vieille Fée estant venu, elle dit, en branlant la teste, encore plus de dépit que de vieillesse, que la Princesse se perceroit la main d’un fuseau & qu’elle en mourroit.
sentences.say: Le rang de la vieille Fée étant venu, elle dit, en branlant la tête, encore plus de dépit que de vieillesse, que la Princesse se percerait la main d’un fuseau et qu’elle en mourrait.
sentences.l: The turn of the old fairy having come, she said, shaking her head, still more from spite than from old age, that the Princess would pierce her hand with a spindle and that she would die of it.
sentences.i: When the old fairy’s turn came, she said, her head shaking more with spite than with age, that the Princess would pierce her hand on a spindle and die of it.
sentences.n: «rang» is ‘turn, place in order’, and «estant venu» ‘being come’ is a participle clause, with 1697 «estant» for «étant». «branler la teste» (modern «tête») is ‘to shake one’s head’, and the French lets the shaking come from age and from spite at once. «se perceroit la main» ‘would pierce herself the hand’ is the French way with parts of the body, where English says ‘her hand’. A «fuseau» ‘spindle’ is the pointed rod onto which spun thread is wound, and «en» in «en mourroit» is ‘of it’.

sentences.t: Ce terrible don fit fremir toute la compagnie, & il n’y eut personne qui ne pleurât.
sentences.say: Ce terrible don fit frémir toute la compagnie, et il n’y eut personne qui ne pleurât.
sentences.l: This terrible gift made the whole company shudder, and there was no one who did not weep.
sentences.i: This terrible gift sent a shudder through the whole company, and there was not one person there who did not weep.
sentences.n: «pleurât» is the imperfect subjunctive again, after «il n’y eut personne qui ne» ‘there was no one who did not’, and «eut» is the passé simple of «avoir». «fit fremir» is ‘made shudder’; «fremir» is modern «frémir».

sentences.t: Dans ce moment, la jeune Fée sortit de derriere la tapisserie, dit tout haut ces paroles : Rassurez-vous, Roi & Reine, vostre fille n’en mourra pas.
sentences.say: Dans ce moment, la jeune Fée sortit de derrière la tapisserie, dit tout haut ces paroles : Rassurez-vous, Roi et Reine, votre fille n’en mourra pas.
sentences.l: At that moment, the young fairy came out from behind the tapestry, [and] said aloud these words: Be reassured, King and Queen, your daughter will not die of it.
sentences.i: At that moment the young fairy came out from behind the tapestry and said aloud: Take heart, King and Queen, your daughter shall not die of it.
sentences.n: The two verbs «sortit» and «dit» stand side by side with only a comma between them, and the literal line supplies ‘and’ in brackets. «Rassurez-vous» ‘reassure yourselves’ is ‘take heart’, and the fairy addresses the parents by rank alone, «Roi & Reine». «vostre» is 1697 for «votre», and «n’en mourra pas» is ‘will not die of it’, the future of «mourir».

sentences.t: Il est vrai que je n’ay pas assez de puissance pour défaire entierement ce que mon ancienne a fait.
sentences.say: Il est vrai que je n’ai pas assez de puissance pour défaire entièrement ce que mon ancienne a fait.
sentences.l: It is true that I have not enough power to undo entirely what my elder has done.
sentences.i: It is true that I have not power enough to undo entirely what my elder has done.
sentences.n: «mon ancienne» ‘my elder’ is the old fairy: «ancien» here is ‘senior, older in standing’, a courteous word even for a rival. «n’ay» is 1697 for «n’ai» ‘I have not’, and «entierement» is «entièrement» ‘entirely’.

sentences.t: La Princesse se percera la main d’un fuseau ; mais, au lieu d’en mourir, elle tombera seulement dans un profond sommeil qui durera cent ans, au bout desquels le fils d’un Roi viendra la réveiller.
sentences.l: The Princess will pierce her hand with a spindle; but, instead of dying of it, she will only fall into a deep sleep which will last a hundred years, at the end of which the son of a King will come to wake her.
sentences.i: The Princess will pierce her hand on a spindle; but instead of dying she will only fall into a deep sleep that will last a hundred years, at the end of which a king’s son will come to wake her.
sentences.n: The young fairy repeats the old one’s words, now in the future («percera», «tombera», «durera», «viendra») where the old fairy’s were reported in the conditional: a sentence she cannot cancel, only soften. «au bout desquels» ‘at the end of which’ looks back to the hundred years. «le fils d’un Roi» is ‘a king’s son’, not yet any particular prince.

sentences.t: Le Roi, pour tâcher d’éviter le malheur annoncé par la vieille, fit publier aussi tost un Edit par lequel il deffendoit à toutes personnes de filer au fuseau, ny d’avoir des fuseaux chez soy, sur peine de la vie.
sentences.say: Le Roi, pour tâcher d’éviter le malheur annoncé par la vieille, fit publier aussi tôt un Édit par lequel il défendait à toutes personnes de filer au fuseau, ni d’avoir des fuseaux chez soi, sur peine de la vie.
sentences.l: The King, to try to avoid the misfortune announced by the old one, had published at once an Edict by which he forbade all persons to spin with the spindle, or to have spindles at home, on pain of life.
sentences.i: To try to avert the misfortune the old fairy had foretold, the King at once had an edict proclaimed forbidding anyone, on pain of death, to spin with a spindle or to keep spindles in the house.
sentences.n: «fit publier» is ‘had proclaimed’, «faire» with an infinitive again. An «Edit» ‘edict’ was a royal law made known in public, and «sur peine de la vie» ‘on pain of life’ is ‘on pain of death’. «aussi tost» is modern «aussitôt» ‘at once’, printed as two words; «deffendoit» (modern «défendait») is ‘forbade’, the older sense of «défendre», beside ‘to defend’; «ny» and «soy» are «ni» and «soi». Spinning thread on a spindle was everyday women’s work, so the ban reaches into every household.

sentences.t: Au bout de quinze ou seize ans, le Roi & la Reine estant allez à une de leurs Maisons de plaisance, il arriva que la jeune Princesse, courant un jour dans le Château, & montant de chambre en chambre, alla jusqu’au haut d’un Donjon dans un petit galletas, où une bonne Vieille estoit seule à filer sa quenoüille.
sentences.say: Au bout de quinze ou seize ans, le Roi et la Reine étant allez à une de leurs Maisons de plaisance, il arriva que la jeune Princesse, courant un jour dans le Château, et montant de chambre en chambre, alla jusqu’au haut d’un Donjon dans un petit galetas, où une bonne Vieille était seule à filer sa quenouille.
sentences.l: At the end of fifteen or sixteen years, the King and the Queen having gone to one of their Houses of pleasure, it happened that the young Princess, running one day through the Castle, and climbing from room to room, went as far as the top of a Keep, into a little garret, where a good Old woman was alone spinning her distaff.
sentences.i: Fifteen or sixteen years later, when the King and Queen had gone to one of their country houses, it so happened that the young Princess, running about the castle one day and climbing from room to room, came up to the top of a tower, into a little garret where a good old woman sat alone spinning at her distaff.
sentences.n: A «Maison de plaisance» ‘house of pleasure’ was a country residence kept for leisure away from the capital. «estant allez» is 1697 for «étant allés» ‘having gone’. A «Donjon» is the great tower or keep of a castle, not a dungeon, and a «galletas» (modern «galetas») is a garret under the roof. The «quenoüille» ‘distaff’ is the staff holding the wool or flax that the spinner draws out into thread and winds onto the spindle. «bonne» ‘good’ before «Vieille» is kindly, and a little condescending, the way one spoke of humble people.

sentences.t: Cette bonne femme n’avoit point ouï parler des deffenses que le roi avoit faites de filer au fuseau.
sentences.say: Cette bonne femme n’avait point ouï parler des défenses que le roi avait faites de filer au fuseau.
sentences.l: This good woman had not heard tell of the prohibitions which the king had made against spinning with the spindle.
sentences.i: This good woman had never heard of the King’s ban on spinning with a spindle.
sentences.n: «ouï parler de» ‘heard speak of’ is ‘heard tell of’; «ouï» is the past participle of «ouïr» ‘to hear’, a verb now rare. «deffenses» (modern «défenses») are ‘prohibitions’, and «faire des défenses de» is ‘to forbid’. «bonne femme» ‘good woman’ is how one spoke of an old countrywoman; the witness prints «roi» here without a capital.

sentences.t: Que faites-vous là, ma bonne femme ? dit la Princesse, Je file, ma belle enfant, luy répondit la vieille, qui ne la connoissoit pas.
sentences.say: Que faites-vous là, ma bonne femme ? dit la Princesse, Je file, ma belle enfant, lui répondit la vieille, qui ne la connaissait pas.
sentences.l: What are you doing there, my good woman? said the Princess. I am spinning, my pretty child, answered her the old woman, who did not know her.
sentences.i: What are you doing there, good woman? said the Princess. I am spinning, my pretty child, the old woman answered, not knowing who she was.
sentences.n: The Princess says «vous» to the old woman, the ordinary courtesy to a stranger; the English stays ‘you’. «ma bonne femme» and «ma belle enfant» ‘my good woman’, ‘my pretty child’ are friendly forms of address. «connoissoit» is 1697 for «connaissait»: she ‘did not know’ her, did not recognise the King’s daughter. The witness sets a comma after «la Princesse» and then a capital on «Je»; the English starts a new sentence there.

sentences.t: Ha ! que cela est joli, reprit la Princesse ; comment faites-vous ? donnez-moy que je voye si j’en ferois bien autant.
sentences.say: Ha ! que cela est joli, reprit la Princesse ; comment faites-vous ? donnez-moi que je voie si j’en ferais bien autant.
sentences.l: Ah! how pretty that is, went on the Princess; how do you do [it]? give [it] to me, that I may see whether I would do as much of it.
sentences.i: Oh, how pretty that is! the Princess went on. How do you do it? Give it to me and let me see if I can do the same.
sentences.n: «que cela est joli» is an exclamation, ‘how pretty that is’, and «Ha» is the exclamation ‘ah’. «reprit» ‘took up again’ is ‘went on, rejoined’. «donnez-moy que je voye» is ‘give me, that I may see’: «voye» is the older form of the subjunctive «voie», and «moy» is «moi». French needs no object after «faites» or «donnez»; the literal line supplies ‘it’ in brackets. «si j’en ferois bien autant» ‘whether I would do as much of it’ has the conditional «ferois» (modern «ferais»).

sentences.t: Elle n’eust pas plutost pris le fuseau, que, comme elle estoit fort vive, un peu estourdie, & que d’ailleurs l’Arrest des Fées l’ordonnoit ainsi, elle s’en perça la main & tomba évanouie.
sentences.say: Elle n’eût pas plutôt pris le fuseau, que, comme elle était fort vive, un peu étourdie, et que d’ailleurs l’Arrêt des Fées l’ordonnait ainsi, elle s’en perça la main et tomba évanouie.
sentences.l: She had no sooner taken the spindle than, as she was very lively, a little heedless, and as besides the Decree of the fairies ordained it so, she pierced her hand with it and fell swooning.
sentences.i: No sooner had she taken hold of the spindle than, being very quick and a little careless, and since the fairies’ decree had so ordained besides, she pierced her hand with it and fell down in a swoon.
sentences.n: «n’eust pas plutost … que» is ‘had no sooner … than’; «eust pris» is a past anterior, with «eust» the 1697 spelling of «eut», and «plutost» is «plutôt». «vive» is ‘lively, quick’, «estourdie» (modern «étourdie») ‘heedless, scatterbrained’. «l’Arrest» (modern «arrêt») is a court’s ruling: the fairies’ gift is treated as a sentence that must be carried out. «perça» and «tomba» are passé simple; in «s’en perça la main» ‘pierced her hand with it’, «en» stands for the spindle, and «évanouie» is ‘in a faint’.

sentences.t: La bonne vieille, bien embarrassée, crie au secours : on vient de tous costez ;
sentences.say: La bonne vieille, bien embarrassée, crie au secours : on vient de tous côtés ;
sentences.l: The good old woman, much at a loss, cries for help: people come from all sides;
sentences.i: The good old woman, at her wits’ end, cries out for help; people come running from every side;
sentences.n: The telling moves into the present tense («crie», «vient»), which makes the alarm immediate, and the English follows it. «bien embarrassée» is ‘greatly at a loss, in great difficulty’, a stronger sense than modern ‘embarrassed’. «on» ‘one’ is everyone at once, ‘people, they’, and «costez» is 1697 for «côtés» ‘sides’.

sentences.t: on jette de l’eau au visage de la princesse, on la délasse, on luy frappe dans les mains, on luy frotte les tempes avec de l’eau de la Reine de Hongrie ; mais rien ne la faisoit revenir.
sentences.say: on jette de l’eau au visage de la princesse, on la délace, on lui frappe dans les mains, on lui frotte les tempes avec de l’eau de la Reine de Hongrie ; mais rien ne la faisait revenir.
sentences.l: they throw water in the face of the princess, they unlace her, they slap her on the hands, they rub her temples with water of the Queen of Hungary; but nothing made her come back.
sentences.i: they throw water in the Princess’s face, unlace her, slap her palms, rub her temples with Hungary water; but nothing would bring her round.
sentences.n: These are the remedies of the time for a faint. «délasse» is the 1697 spelling of «délace» ‘unlaces’: they loosen her laced bodice so that she can breathe; modern «délasser» is another verb, ‘to refresh, to rest’. «l’eau de la Reine de Hongrie», in English ‘Hungary water’, was a well-known distilled water of rosemary in spirit, used as a scent and as a restorative. «ne la faisoit revenir» ‘made her come back’ returns to the past, in the imperfect: nothing they tried was of use.

sentences.t: Alors le Roy, qui estoit monté au bruit, se souvint de la prédiction des fées, et, jugeant bien qu’il falloit que cela arrivast, puisque les Fées l’avoient dit, fit mettre la Princesse dans le plus bel appartement du Palais, sur un lit en broderie d’or & d’argent.
sentences.say: Alors le Roi, qui était monté au bruit, se souvint de la prédiction des fées, et, jugeant bien qu’il fallait que cela arrivât, puisque les Fées l’avaient dit, fit mettre la Princesse dans le plus bel appartement du Palais, sur un lit en broderie d’or et d’argent.
sentences.l: Then the King, who had come up at the noise, remembered the prediction of the fairies, and, judging rightly that it must be that this should happen, since the fairies had said it, had the Princess put in the finest apartment of the Palace, on a bed in embroidery of gold and silver.
sentences.i: Then the King, who had come up at the commotion, remembered the fairies’ prediction, and, judging rightly that this was bound to happen since the fairies had said so, had the Princess laid in the finest apartment of the palace, on a bed embroidered with gold and silver.
sentences.n: «il falloit que cela arrivast» ‘it was needful that this should happen’ has «arrivast» (modern «arrivât»), imperfect subjunctive after «il falloit que». «se souvint» is the passé simple of «se souvenir» ‘to remember’. «Roy» here and «Roi» elsewhere are the same word; the book uses both spellings. An «appartement» in a palace was a suite of rooms, not a single room.

sentences.t: On eût dit d’un Ange, tant elle estoit belle : car son évanouissement n’avoit pas osté les couleurs vives de son teint : ses joues estoient incarnates, & ses levres comme du corail ;
sentences.say: On eût dit d’un Ange, tant elle était belle : car son évanouissement n’avait pas ôté les couleurs vives de son teint : ses joues étaient incarnates, et ses lèvres comme du corail ;
sentences.l: One would have said [it was] an Angel, so beautiful she was: for her swoon had not taken away the bright colours of her complexion: her cheeks were rosy, and her lips like coral;
sentences.i: She might have been an angel, she was so beautiful; for her swoon had not taken the bright colour from her complexion: her cheeks were rosy and her lips like coral;
sentences.n: «On eût dit d’un Ange» is ‘one would have said (it was) an angel’: «eût dit» is the pluperfect subjunctive used, as literary French still uses it, for ‘would have said’, and the «d’» ‘of’ is the older construction, where modern French says «on eût dit un ange»; the literal line supplies ‘it was’ in brackets. «tant elle estoit belle» is ‘so much was she beautiful’. «osté» is 1697 for «ôté» ‘taken away’. «incarnat», from a word for ‘flesh’, is a bright rosy red, the colour of a healthy complexion.

sentences.t: elle avoit seulement les yeux fermez, mais on l’entendoit respirer doucement : ce qui faisoit voir qu’elle n’estoit pas morte.
sentences.say: elle avait seulement les yeux fermés, mais on l’entendait respirer doucement : ce qui faisait voir qu’elle n’était pas morte.
sentences.l: she had only the eyes closed, but one could hear her breathe softly: which made it plain that she was not dead.
sentences.i: only her eyes were shut, but she could be heard breathing gently, which showed that she was not dead.
sentences.n: «avoit … les yeux fermez» ‘had the eyes closed’ is the French way with parts of the body, where English says ‘her eyes’; «fermez» is 1697 for «fermés». «faisoit voir» ‘made (one) see’ is ‘showed’. The imperfects («avoit», «entendoit», «faisoit», «estoit») describe the scene as it lay, not events one after another.

sentences.t: Le Roi ordonna qu’on la laissast dormir en repos, jusqu’à ce que son heure de se réveiller fust venue.
sentences.say: Le Roi ordonna qu’on la laissât dormir en repos, jusqu’à ce que son heure de se réveiller fût venue.
sentences.l: The King ordered that they should let her sleep in peace, until her hour to wake should be come.
sentences.i: The King gave orders that she be left to sleep in peace until her hour to awaken had come.
sentences.n: Two more subjunctives: «laissast» (modern «laissât») is the imperfect subjunctive after «ordonner que» ‘to order that’, and «fust venue» (modern «fût venue») is a pluperfect subjunctive after «jusqu’à ce que» ‘until’, built with «fust», the imperfect subjunctive of «estre».

sentences.t: La bonne Fée qui luy avoit sauvé la vie en la condamnant à dormir cent ans estoit dans le Royaume de Mataquin, à douze mille lieuës de là, lorsque l’accident arriva à la Princesse ;
sentences.say: La bonne Fée qui lui avait sauvé la vie en la condamnant à dormir cent ans était dans le Royaume de Mataquin, à douze mille lieues de là, lorsque l’accident arriva à la Princesse ;
sentences.l: The good fairy who had saved her life by condemning her to sleep a hundred years was in the Kingdom of Mataquin, twelve thousand leagues from there, when the accident happened to the Princess;
sentences.i: The good fairy who had saved her life by condemning her to sleep for a hundred years was in the kingdom of Mataquin, twelve thousand leagues away, when the accident befell the Princess;
sentences.n: «Mataquin» is a far-off kingdom that seems to be the tale’s own invention, and its name stays as the French prints it. «lieuës» is the 1697 spelling of «lieues» ‘leagues’; at two and a half to three miles to the league, twelve thousand leagues is farther than the whole way round the earth, a fairy-tale distance. «luy avoit sauvé la vie» is ‘had saved her life’, with «luy» ‘to her’ where English says ‘her’.

sentences.t: mais elle en fut avertie en un instant par un petit Nain qui avoit des bottes de sept lieues (c’estoit des bottes avec lesquelles on faisoit sept lieues d’une seule enjambée).
sentences.say: mais elle en fut avertie en un instant par un petit Nain qui avait des bottes de sept lieues (c’était des bottes avec lesquelles on faisait sept lieues d’une seule enjambée).
sentences.l: but she was warned of it in an instant by a little dwarf who had the boots of seven leagues (they were boots with which one covered seven leagues in a single stride).
sentences.i: but she was told of it in an instant by a little dwarf who had the seven-league boots (these were boots in which one went seven leagues at a single stride).
sentences.n: «lieuës» is the 1697 spelling of «lieues» ‘leagues’; a league was a measure of road distance that varied from place to place, roughly two and a half to three miles. The Sleeping Beauty explains the boots in its own words, printing «lieues» without the diaeresis: boots with which one covered seven leagues in a single stride. In Little Thumb they are also «Fées», ‘enchanted’, and fit whoever puts them on. «des bottes» is strictly ‘some boots’, a pair of such boots, not a famous pair; the English gives them the name such boots are known by. «en fut avertie» ‘was warned of it’ is the passé simple of the passive, and in «c’estoit des bottes» ‘it was boots’ a singular verb introduces a plural, as French still allows. «enjambée» is ‘stride’, from «jambe» ‘leg’.

sentences.t: La Fée partit aussi tost, & on la vit, au bout d’une heure, arriver dans un chariot tout de feu, traisné par des dragons.
sentences.say: La Fée partit aussi tôt, et on la vit, au bout d’une heure, arriver dans un chariot tout de feu, traîné par des dragons.
sentences.l: The fairy set out at once, and they saw her, at the end of an hour, arrive in a chariot all of fire, drawn by dragons.
sentences.i: The fairy set off at once, and an hour later she was seen arriving in a chariot all of fire, drawn by dragons.
sentences.n: «tout de feu» ‘all of fire’ is ‘blazing, fiery’. «traisné» is 1697 for «traîné» ‘drawn, pulled’, and «aussi tost» is «aussitôt» ‘at once’. «partit» is the passé simple of «partir» ‘to set out’.

sentences.t: Le Roi luy alla presenter la main à la descente du chariot.
sentences.say: Le Roi lui alla présenter la main à la descente du chariot.
sentences.l: The King went to present her his hand at her getting down from the chariot.
sentences.i: The King went to offer her his hand as she stepped down from the chariot.
sentences.n: Offering one’s hand to help a lady down from a carriage was a courtesy of rank, and here a king pays it to a fairy. «luy alla presenter» sets the pronoun before «alla», the usual 1697 order, where modern French says «alla lui présenter». «la main» ‘the hand’ is ‘his hand’.

sentences.t: Elle approuva tout ce qu’il avoit fait ; mais, comme elle estoit grandement prévoyante, elle pensa que, quand la Princesse viendrait à se réveiller, elle seroit bien embarassée toute seule dans ce vieux château : voicy ce qu’elle fit.
sentences.say: Elle approuva tout ce qu’il avait fait ; mais, comme elle était grandement prévoyante, elle pensa que, quand la Princesse viendrait à se réveiller, elle serait bien embarrassée toute seule dans ce vieux château : voici ce qu’elle fit.
sentences.l: She approved all that he had done; but, as she was greatly far-sighted, she thought that, when the Princess should come to wake, she would be much at a loss all alone in this old castle: here is what she did.
sentences.i: She approved of everything he had done; but, being a fairy of great foresight, she reflected that when the Princess came to wake she would be sorely at a loss all alone in that old castle, and this is what she did.
sentences.n: «prévoyante» is ‘far-sighted, provident’, from «prévoir» ‘to foresee’. «viendrait à se réveiller» ‘would come to wake’ is a future seen from the past; the witness prints «viendrait» with the modern ending beside «seroit», and «embarassée» with one «r» where the old woman was «embarrassée» with two; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «voicy» is 1697 for «voici» ‘here is’.

sentences.t: Elle toucha de sa baguette tout ce qui estoit dans ce Chasteau (hors le Roi & la Reine) : Gouvernantes, Filles-d’Honneur, Femmes-de-Chambre, Gentils-Hommes, Officiers, Maistres d’Hostel, Cuisiniers, Marmitons, Galopins, Gardes, Suisses, Pages, Valets-de-pied ;
sentences.say: Elle toucha de sa baguette tout ce qui était dans ce Château (hors le Roi et la Reine) : Gouvernantes, Filles-d’Honneur, Femmes-de-Chambre, Gentilshommes, Officiers, Maîtres d’Hôtel, Cuisiniers, Marmitons, Galopins, Gardes, Suisses, Pages, Valets-de-pied ;
sentences.l: She touched with her wand all that was in this Castle (except the King and the Queen): Governesses, Maids-of-Honour, Chambermaids, Gentlemen, Officers, Stewards, Cooks, Scullions, Errand-boys, Guards, Swiss, Pages, Footmen;
sentences.i: She touched with her wand everyone in the castle, except the King and Queen: governesses, maids of honour, chambermaids, gentlemen, household officers, stewards, cooks, scullions, errand boys, guards, Swiss guards, pages, footmen;
sentences.n: A great household in its ranks, from the governesses down to the footmen; «hors» is ‘except’. «Filles-d’Honneur» are maids of honour, young women of good family attending a princess, and «Femmes-de-Chambre» her chambermaids, who dressed her and kept her rooms. «Gentils-Hommes» (modern «gentilshommes») are men of noble birth in a prince’s service, and «Officiers» are officers of the household. A «Maistre d’Hostel», ‘steward’, is the officer in charge of a great household’s table. «Marmitons» are kitchen boys, from «marmite» ‘cooking pot’, and «Galopins» errand boys, from «galoper» ‘to gallop’. The «Suisses» are Swiss soldiers, whom royal and princely houses kept as guards and doorkeepers. «Valets-de-pied» are footmen. The hyphens and capitals are the 1697 printer’s.

sentences.t: elle toucha aussi tous les chevaux qui estoient dans les Ecuries, avec les Palfreniers, les gros mâtins de basse-cour, & la petite Pouffe, petite chienne de la Princesse, qui estoit auprés d’elle sur son lit.
sentences.say: elle toucha aussi tous les chevaux qui étaient dans les Écuries, avec les Palefreniers, les gros mâtins de basse-cour, et la petite Pouffe, petite chienne de la Princesse, qui était auprès d’elle sur son lit.
sentences.l: she touched also all the horses that were in the Stables, with the Grooms, the big mastiffs of the yard, and the little Pouffe, little dog of the Princess, who was near her on her bed.
sentences.i: she touched all the horses in the stables too, with the grooms, the great watchdogs of the yard, and little Pouffe, the Princess’s little dog, who lay beside her on the bed.
sentences.n: «Pouffe» is the little dog’s name and stays French; what it was meant to suggest is not certain. «chienne» is a female dog. «mâtins» are big, heavy guard dogs, and the «basse-cour» is the service yard where poultry and animals were kept. «Palfreniers» (modern «palefreniers») are grooms, and «Ecuries» (modern «écuries») stables, printed without an accent on the capital.

sentences.t: Dés qu’elle les eust touchez, ils s’endormirent tous, pour ne se réveiller qu’en mesme temps que leur Maistresse, afin d’estre tout prests à la servir quand elle en auroit besoin :
sentences.say: Dès qu’elle les eût touchez, ils s’endormirent tous, pour ne se réveiller qu’en même temps que leur Maîtresse, afin d’être tout prêts à la servir quand elle en aurait besoin :
sentences.l: As soon as she had touched them, they all fell asleep, to wake only at the same time as their Mistress, so as to be quite ready to serve her when she should have need of it:
sentences.i: As soon as she had touched them they all fell asleep, not to wake until their mistress woke, so that they would be ready to wait on her when she needed them:
sentences.n: «eust touchez» is a past anterior, ‘had touched’, with 1697 «eust» for «eut» and «touchez» for «touchés». «ne … qu’en mesme temps que» is ‘not … except at the same time as’, that is, ‘only when’; «mesme» is «même», and «estre tout prests» is «être tout prêts» ‘to be all ready’. «Maistresse» (modern «maîtresse») is the mistress of the household, their lady. «en» in «en auroit besoin» stands for their service.

sentences.t: les broches mêmes qui estoient au feu, toutes pleines de perdrix & de faysans, s’endormirent, & le feu aussi.
sentences.say: les broches mêmes qui étaient au feu, toutes pleines de perdrix et de faisans, s’endormirent, et le feu aussi.
sentences.l: the spits even that were at the fire, all full of partridges and pheasants, fell asleep, and the fire too.
sentences.i: even the spits over the fire, loaded with partridges and pheasants, fell asleep, and the fire as well.
sentences.n: «mêmes» after a noun is ‘even, the very’. A «broche» is a roasting spit turned before an open fire; the spell stops the roasting where it stands. «faysans» is 1697 for «faisans» ‘pheasants’, and «s’endormirent» ‘fell asleep’ is passé simple.

sentences.t: Tout cela se fit en un moment : les Fées n’estoient pas longues à leur besogne.
sentences.say: Tout cela se fit en un moment : les Fées n’étaient pas longues à leur besogne.
sentences.l: All that was done in a moment: the fairies were not long at their work.
sentences.i: All this was done in a moment; fairies were not long about their work.
sentences.n: «se fit» ‘made itself’ is the reflexive used as a passive, ‘was done’. The aside speaks of fairies in general, and its imperfect («n’estoient») gives it the sound of a saying; «besogne» is ‘task, work’.

sentences.t: Alors le Roi & la Reine aprés avoir baisé leur chere enfant sans qu’elle s’éveillast, sortirent du chasteau, & firent publier des deffenses à qui que ce soit d’en approcher.
sentences.say: Alors le Roi et la Reine après avoir baisé leur chère enfant sans qu’elle s’éveillât, sortirent du château, et firent publier des défenses à qui que ce soit d’en approcher.
sentences.l: Then the King and the Queen, after having kissed their dear child without her waking, went out of the castle, and had prohibitions proclaimed to anyone whatever against coming near it.
sentences.i: Then the King and Queen, having kissed their dear child without waking her, left the castle and had it proclaimed that no one whatsoever was to come near it.
sentences.n: «baiser» is here plainly ‘to kiss’; as a verb it has since taken a vulgar sense, and modern French says «embrasser». «s’éveillast» (modern «s’éveillât») is the imperfect subjunctive after «sans que» ‘without’. «à qui que ce soit» is ‘to anyone at all’, and «en approcher» ‘to come near it’, «en» standing for the castle.

sentences.t: Ces deffenses n’estoient pas necessaires, car il crut dans un quart d’heure tout au tour du parc une si grande quantité de grands arbres & de petits, de ronces & d’épines entrelassées les unes dans les autres, que beste ny homme n’y auroit pû passer :
sentences.say: Ces défenses n’étaient pas nécessaires, car il crut dans un quart d’heure tout au tour du parc une si grande quantité de grands arbres et de petits, de ronces et d’épines entrelacées les unes dans les autres, que bête ni homme n’y aurait pu passer :
sentences.l: These prohibitions were not necessary, for there grew in a quarter of an hour all around the park so great a quantity of big trees and of small, of brambles and thorns interlaced one with another, that neither beast nor man could have passed through:
sentences.i: These prohibitions were not needed, for within a quarter of an hour there grew up all around the park such a mass of trees great and small, of brambles and thorns twined one into another, that neither beast nor man could have got through,
sentences.n: «il crut» is ‘there grew’: «crut» here is the passé simple of «croître» ‘to grow’, not of «croire» ‘to believe’, with the impersonal «il» as in «il y avoit»; modern French gives the verb for growing the circumflex, «crût», and the book did the reverse a few sentences back, printing «crût» for ‘believed’. «tout au tour» is modern «tout autour» ‘all around’. «entrelassées» (modern «entrelacées») is ‘interlaced’. «beste ny homme n’y auroit pû passer» is ‘beast nor man could not have passed there’: «ny» with «ne» does the work of ‘neither … nor’, and «beste», «ny», «pû» are 1697 for «bête», «ni», «pu».

sentences.t: en sorte qu’on ne voyoit plus que le haut des Tours du Chasteau, encore n’estoit-ce que de bien loin.
sentences.say: en sorte qu’on ne voyait plus que le haut des Tours du Château, encore n’était-ce que de bien loin.
sentences.l: so that one no longer saw anything but the top of the Towers of the Castle, and even that was only from very far off.
sentences.i: so that nothing more could be seen but the tops of the castle towers, and even those only from a great way off.
sentences.n: «ne … plus que» is ‘no longer anything but’, and «voyoit» is 1697 for «voyait». «encore» at the head of a clause, with verb and subject turned round («n’estoit-ce»), is ‘and even then’: ‘and even that was only from far off’.

sentences.t: On ne douta point que la fée n’eust encore fait là un tour de son métier, afin que la Princesse, pendant qu’elle dormiroit, n’eust rien à craindre des Curieux.
sentences.say: On ne douta point que la fée n’eût encore fait là un tour de son métier, afin que la Princesse, pendant qu’elle dormirait, n’eût rien à craindre des Curieux.
sentences.l: They did not doubt at all that the fairy had once more done there a trick of her trade, so that the Princess, while she slept, should have nothing to fear from the Curious.
sentences.i: No one doubted that this was another stroke of the fairy’s craft, so that the Princess would have nothing to fear from the curious while she slept.
sentences.n: «un tour de son métier» ‘a turn of her trade’ is a feat of her craft, «tour» being ‘trick, feat’. After «ne douter point que» French sets a «ne» in the clause that follows without making it negative («n’eust … fait» is ‘had done’), while the «ne … rien» after «afin que» is a true negative, ‘should have nothing’; «n’eust … fait» is a pluperfect subjunctive and «n’eust rien» an imperfect subjunctive, both «eust» being 1697 for «eût». «dormiroit» is «dormirait». The «Curieux» are ‘the curious’, meddlers and sightseers.

sentences.t: Au bout de cent ans, le fils du roi qui regnoit alors, & qui estoit d’une autre famille que la princesse endormie, estant allé à la chasse de ce costé-là, demanda ce que c’estoit que des Tours qu’il voyoit au-dessus d’un grand bois fort épais, chacun luy répondit selon qu’il en avoit ouï parler.
sentences.say: Au bout de cent ans, le fils du roi qui régnait alors, et qui était d’une autre famille que la princesse endormie, étant allé à la chasse de ce côté-là, demanda ce que c’était que des Tours qu’il voyait au-dessus d’un grand bois fort épais, chacun lui répondit selon qu’il en avait ouï parler.
sentences.l: At the end of a hundred years, the son of the king who reigned then, and who was of another family than the sleeping princess, being gone hunting on that side, asked what they were, the Towers that he saw above a great wood, very thick; each one answered him according as he had heard tell of it.
sentences.i: When a hundred years had gone by, the son of the king then reigning, who was of a different family from the sleeping Princess, went hunting in those parts and asked what the towers were that he could see above a great and very dense wood. Each person told him whatever he had heard.
sentences.n: «regnoit», «voyoit», «avoit» are the 1697 imperfect in «-oit» (modern «-ait»), «estant» is «étant», «costé» «côté» and «luy» «lui»; «demanda» and «répondit» are passé simple, the tale’s narrative past. «ce que c’estoit que des Tours» is literally ‘what it was, some towers’: «ce que c’est que» before a noun is the ordinary French way of asking what a thing is. «ouï» is the past participle of «ouïr» ‘to hear’, and «ouïr parler de» is ‘to hear tell of’. The 1697 punctuation runs the question and the answers together with a comma; the English gives them a stop. «une autre famille» is another royal line: the sleeping Princess’s house no longer reigns.

sentences.t: Les uns disoient que c’estoit un vieux Château où il revenoit des Esprits ; les autres, que tous les Sorciers de la Contrée y faisoient leur sabbat.
sentences.say: Les uns disaient que c’était un vieux Château où il revenait des Esprits ; les autres, que tous les Sorciers de la Contrée y faisaient leur sabbat.
sentences.l: Some said that it was an old Castle where there came back Spirits; the others, that all the Sorcerers of the Region held their sabbath there.
sentences.i: Some said it was an old castle haunted by ghosts; others, that all the sorcerers of the country held their sabbath there.
sentences.n: «Les uns … les autres» is ‘some … others’. «il revenoit des Esprits» is impersonal, ‘there came back spirits’: «revenir» ‘to come back’ is the verb of ghosts, and a ghost is still «un revenant» ‘one who comes back’. The «sabbat» was the nocturnal gathering of witches in popular belief. The book prints «Château» here and «Chasteau» a few lines on; they are one word.

sentences.t: La plus commune opinion estoit qu’un Ogre y demeuroit, & que là il emportoit tous les enfans qu’il pouvoit attraper, pour les pouvoir manger à son aise & sans qu’on le pust suivre, ayant seul le pouvoir de se faire un passage au travers du bois.
sentences.say: La plus commune opinion était qu’un Ogre y demeurait, et que là il emportait tous les enfants qu’il pouvait attraper, pour les pouvoir manger à son aise et sans qu’on le pût suivre, ayant seul le pouvoir de se faire un passage au travers du bois.
sentences.l: The most common opinion was that an Ogre lived there, and that there he carried off all the children that he could catch, so as to be able to eat them at his ease and without anyone being able to follow him, having alone the power to make himself a passage through the wood.
sentences.i: The most widely held view was that an Ogre lived there and carried off to it every child he could catch, so that he could eat them at his leisure with no one able to follow him, since he alone had the power to make his way through the wood.
sentences.n: An «Ogre» is the man-eating giant of folk tale. «pour les pouvoir manger» sets the pronoun before «pouvoir», the usual 1697 order, where modern French says «pour pouvoir les manger». «pust» (modern «pût») is the imperfect subjunctive after «sans que» ‘without’. «enfans» is the 1697 spelling of «enfants», and «au travers du» is ‘through the’.

sentences.t: Le prince ne sçavoit qu’en croire, lors qu’un vieux Paysan prit la parole & luy dit :
sentences.say: Le prince ne savait qu’en croire, lors qu’un vieux Paysan prit la parole et lui dit :
sentences.l: The prince knew not what to believe of it, when an old Peasant took the word and said to him:
sentences.i: The Prince did not know what to believe, when an old countryman spoke up and said to him:
sentences.n: «ne sçavoit qu’en croire» is ‘did not know what to believe of it’, with «ne» alone, and no «pas», negating «savoir», as it often does. «sçavoit» is the 1697 spelling of «savait», its «ç» owed to a mistaken link with Latin «scire» ‘to know’. «lors que» is modern «lorsque» ‘when’, and «prendre la parole» ‘to take the word’ is ‘to begin to speak’. «Paysan» carries the capital the book gives many common nouns; the spelling with «y» is still the modern one.

sentences.t: Mon Prince, il y a plus de cinquante ans que j’ay ouï dire à mon pere qu’il y avoit dans ce Chasteau une Princesse, la plus belle du monde ; qu’elle y devoit dormir cent ans, & qu’elle seroit réveillée par le fils d’un Roi, à qui elle estoit reservée.
sentences.say: Mon Prince, il y a plus de cinquante ans que j’ai ouï dire à mon père qu’il y avait dans ce Château une Princesse, la plus belle du monde ; qu’elle y devait dormir cent ans, et qu’elle serait réveillée par le fils d’un Roi, à qui elle était réservée.
sentences.l: My Prince, it is more than fifty years since I heard my father say that there was in this Castle a Princess, the most beautiful of the world; that she was to sleep there a hundred years, and that she would be woken by the son of a King, for whom she was reserved.
sentences.i: My Prince, more than fifty years ago I heard my father say that there was a princess in this castle, the most beautiful in the world; that she was to sleep there for a hundred years, and would be woken by a king’s son, for whom she was destined.
sentences.n: «il y a plus de cinquante ans que» is ‘it is more than fifty years since’, the French way of measuring time back from now. In «ouï dire à mon pere» the «à» marks the one speaking: ‘heard my father say’. «devoit dormir» is ‘was to sleep’, «devoir» of what is fated, and «reservée» is ‘kept, set aside’ for the king’s son. «j’ay» is the 1697 spelling of «j’ai», and «pere» of «père».

sentences.t: Le jeune Prince à ce discours se sentit tout de feu ;
sentences.l: The young Prince at this speech felt himself all on fire;
sentences.i: At these words the young Prince felt himself all aflame;
sentences.n: «se sentit» is the passé simple of «se sentir» ‘to feel (oneself)’, and «tout de feu» ‘all of fire’ is burning with ardour. «discours» is any speech or talk, not a formal oration.

sentences.t: il crut sans balancer qu’il mettroit fin à une si belle avanture, & poussé par l’amour & par la gloire, il résolut de voir sur le champ ce qui en estoit.
sentences.say: il crut sans balancer qu’il mettrait fin à une si belle aventure, et poussé par l’amour et par la gloire, il résolut de voir sur le champ ce qui en était.
sentences.l: he believed without wavering that he would put an end to so fine an adventure, and pushed by love and by glory, he resolved to see on the spot what there was of it.
sentences.i: he believed without a moment’s hesitation that he would bring so fine an adventure to its end, and, spurred on by love and by glory, he resolved to see at once what truth there was in it.
sentences.n: «balancer», to swing like a pair of scales, is ‘to waver, hesitate’ in 1697, so «sans balancer» is ‘without hesitating’. «crut» is the passé simple of «croire», «mettroit» (modern «mettrait») a conditional, and «avanture» the 1697 spelling of «aventure». «sur le champ» ‘on the field’ is ‘at once’ (modern «sur-le-champ»), and «voir ce qui en estoit» is ‘to see how matters stood’. Love and «la gloire», the renown won by a brave deed, are the hero’s two spurs in the romances of the time.

sentences.t: À peine s’avança-t-il vers le bois que tous ces grands arbres, ces ronces, & ces épines s’écarterent d’elles-mesmes pour le laisser passer :
sentences.say: À peine s’avança-t-il vers le bois que tous ces grands arbres, ces ronces, et ces épines s’écartèrent d’elles-mêmes pour le laisser passer :
sentences.l: Scarcely did he advance toward the wood when all those great trees, those brambles, and those thorns drew apart of themselves to let him pass:
sentences.i: Scarcely had he set out toward the wood when all those great trees, brambles and thorns parted of their own accord to let him through;
sentences.n: «À peine … que» is ‘scarcely … when’, and like English ‘scarcely did he’ it puts the subject after the verb: «s’avança-t-il», with a «t» slipped in between two vowels for the sound. «s’écarterent» is passé simple (modern «s’écartèrent»), and «d’elles-mesmes» ‘of themselves’ is feminine to agree with «ronces» and «épines», the nearest nouns; «mesme» is the 1697 spelling of «même».

sentences.t: il marche vers le Chasteau qu’il voyoit au bout d’une grande avenuë où il entra, & ce qui le surprit un peu, il vit que personne de ses gens ne l’avoit pû suivre, parce que les arbres s’estoient rapprochez dés qu’il avoit esté passé.
sentences.say: il marche vers le Château qu’il voyait au bout d’une grande avenue où il entra, et ce qui le surprit un peu, il vit que personne de ses gens ne l’avait pu suivre, parce que les arbres s’étaient rapprochez dès qu’il avait été passé.
sentences.l: he walks toward the Castle that he saw at the end of a great avenue which he entered, and what surprised him a little, he saw that none of his people had been able to follow him, because the trees had drawn together again as soon as he was past.
sentences.i: he walks toward the castle, which he could see at the end of a great avenue; he entered the avenue and, what surprised him a little, saw that none of his men had been able to follow him, because the trees had closed up again as soon as he was through.
sentences.n: The narration slips into the present, «il marche», and back into the passé simple, «il entra», «il vit»; the English follows it. «personne de ses gens» is ‘none of his people’, the attendants who rode out with him. «avoit esté passé» is a doubled compound tense of «passer», built on «il est passé» ‘he is past, has gone by’: it means ‘had got past’ and is not the passive ‘had been passed’. «avenuë» is the 1697 spelling of «avenue», «pû» of «pu», «rapprochez» of «rapprochés» and «dés» of «dès» ‘as soon as’.

sentences.t: Il ne laissa pas de continuer son chemin : un Prince jeune & amoureux est toûjours vaillant.
sentences.say: Il ne laissa pas de continuer son chemin : un Prince jeune et amoureux est toujours vaillant.
sentences.l: He did not leave off continuing his way: a Prince young and in love is always valiant.
sentences.i: He went on his way nonetheless: a young prince in love is always brave.
sentences.n: «ne pas laisser de» with an infinitive is ‘not to fail to’, so «Il ne laissa pas de continuer» is ‘he went on all the same’. The second half is a maxim in the present tense, the narrator speaking over the Prince’s shoulder. «toûjours» is the 1697 spelling of «toujours».

sentences.t: Il entra dans une grande avancour, où tout ce qu’il vit d’abord estoit capable de le glacer de crainte :
sentences.say: Il entra dans une grande avant-cour, où tout ce qu’il vit d’abord était capable de le glacer de crainte :
sentences.l: He entered into a great forecourt, where all that he saw at first was capable of freezing him with fear:
sentences.i: He came into a great forecourt, where everything he first set eyes on was enough to freeze him with fear:
sentences.n: «avancour» is ‘forecourt’ (modern «avant-cour»), the outer court of a great house, before its main court. «d’abord» here is ‘at first sight, straight away’, and «estre capable de» ‘to be such as to’.

sentences.t: c’estoit un silence affreux, l’image de la mort s’y presentoit par tout, & ce n’estoit que des corps étendus d’hommes & d’animaux, qui paroissoient morts.
sentences.say: c’était un silence affreux, l’image de la mort s’y présentait par tout, et ce n’était que des corps étendus d’hommes et d’animaux, qui paraissaient morts.
sentences.l: it was a frightful silence, the image of death presented itself there everywhere, and it was nothing but stretched-out bodies of men and of animals, which seemed dead.
sentences.i: there was a dreadful silence, the image of death met him on every side, and there was nothing to be seen but the bodies of men and animals lying stretched out as if dead.
sentences.n: «ce n’estoit que» uses «ne … que» ‘nothing but’, and keeps a singular «c’estoit» before a plural noun, as French often did. «affreux» keeps its full force here, ‘frightful’, not merely ‘awful’. «paroissoient» is the 1697 spelling of «paraissaient» ‘seemed’, and «par tout» is modern «partout».

sentences.t: Il reconnut pourtant bien au nez bourgeonnez & à la face vermeille des Suisses, qu’ils n’estoient qu’endormis,
sentences.say: Il reconnut pourtant bien au nez bourgeonné et à la face vermeille des Suisses, qu’ils n’étaient qu’endormis,
sentences.l: He made out nevertheless quite well, by the pimpled nose and by the ruddy face of the Swiss, that they were only asleep,
sentences.i: Yet he could tell well enough, from the pimpled noses and ruddy faces of the Swiss guards, that they were only asleep,
sentences.n: The «Suisses» were Swiss soldiers hired as guards and door-keepers by kings and great lords, and they had a name for drinking: hence the red faces and the budding noses. «bourgeonnez» ‘pimpled’, from «bourgeon» ‘bud’, has the plural ending «-ez» (modern «-és») although «au nez» is singular; it may think of each guard’s nose or may be a slip, and the idiomatic English says ‘noses’ either way. «reconnut» is the passé simple of «reconnoistre» (modern «reconnaître») ‘to make out’, and «ne … que» is ‘only’ again.

sentences.t: & leurs tasses où il y avoit encore quelques goutes de vin, montroient assez qu’ils s’estoient endormis en beuvant.
sentences.say: et leurs tasses où il y avait encore quelques gouttes de vin, montraient assez qu’ils s’étaient endormis en buvant.
sentences.l: and their cups, where there were still some drops of wine, showed well enough that they had fallen asleep while drinking.
sentences.i: and their cups, which still held a few drops of wine, showed plainly enough that they had fallen asleep as they drank.
sentences.n: «en beuvant» is ‘while drinking’, the gerund of «boire» in its older form «beuvant» (modern «buvant»); «goutes» is the 1697 spelling of «gouttes» ‘drops’. «il y avoit» ‘there there-had’ is ‘there were’, and «assez» here is ‘sufficiently, plainly enough’.

sentences.t: Il passe une grande cour pavée de marbre, il monte l’escalier, il entre dans la salle des Gardes qui estoient rangez en haye, la carabine sur l’épaule, & ronflans de leur mieux.
sentences.say: Il passe une grande cour pavée de marbre, il monte l’escalier, il entre dans la salle des Gardes qui étaient rangez en haie, la carabine sur l’épaule, et ronflants de leur mieux.
sentences.l: He passes a great court paved with marble, he climbs the staircase, he enters into the hall of the Guards, who were ranged in a hedge, the carbine on the shoulder, and snoring their best.
sentences.i: He crosses a great marble-paved court, climbs the staircase and enters the guardroom, where the guards stood drawn up in a line, carbines on their shoulders, snoring with all their might.
sentences.n: The present tense returns, in short clauses that follow the Prince step by step. «en haye» (modern «en haie») ‘in a hedge’ is ‘in a line’, soldiers drawn up in a row, and a «carabine» is a short firearm carried by guards and horsemen. «ronflans», for modern «ronflant», is a present participle made plural to agree with «Gardes», as 1697 French still allowed, and «rangez» is «rangés».

sentences.t: Il traverse plusieurs chambres pleines de Gentilshommes & de Dames, dormans tous, les uns debout, les autres assis ;
sentences.say: Il traverse plusieurs chambres pleines de Gentilshommes et de Dames, dormants tous, les uns debout, les autres assis ;
sentences.l: He crosses several rooms full of Gentlemen and of Ladies, sleeping all, some standing, the others seated;
sentences.i: He passes through several rooms full of gentlemen and ladies, all of them asleep, some standing, some sitting;
sentences.n: «Gentilshommes» are men of noble birth, and «Dames» the ladies of a court; a «chambre» is any room of a great house, not only a bedroom. «dormans» is another plural present participle (modern «dormant»).

sentences.t: il entre dans une chambre toute dorée, & il vit sur un lit, dont les rideaux estoient ouverts de tous côtez, le plus beau spectacle qu’il eut jamais veu :
sentences.say: il entre dans une chambre toute dorée, et il vit sur un lit, dont les rideaux étaient ouverts de tous côtés, le plus beau spectacle qu’il eut jamais vu :
sentences.l: he enters into a room all gilded, and he saw on a bed, whose curtains were open on all sides, the most beautiful sight that he had ever seen:
sentences.i: he comes into a room gilded all over, and there on a bed, its curtains drawn back on every side, he saw the loveliest sight he had ever beheld:
sentences.n: The present «il entre» gives way to the passé simple «il vit» at the moment of sight. A great bed was hung with curtains all round, closed at night; these stand open. «eut» stands for «eût», the pluperfect subjunctive after a superlative, printed without its circumflex as the book often prints it; «veu» is «vu» and «côtez» «côtés».

sentences.t: Une Princesse qui paroissoit avoir quinze ou seize ans, & dont l’éclat resplendissant avoit quelque chose de lumineux & de divin.
sentences.say: Une Princesse qui paraissait avoir quinze ou seize ans, et dont l’éclat resplendissant avait quelque chose de lumineux et de divin.
sentences.l: A Princess who appeared to have fifteen or sixteen years, and whose resplendent brilliance had something of the luminous and of the divine.
sentences.i: A princess who seemed to be fifteen or sixteen years old, and whose shining radiance had about it something of light and of the divine.
sentences.n: «avoir quinze ou seize ans» ‘to have fifteen or sixteen years’ is how French gives an age: she looks just as old as when she fell asleep. «éclat» is ‘brilliance, radiance’, and «quelque chose de» with an adjective is ‘something (luminous)’. The capital on «Une» after the colon is the printer’s.

sentences.t: Il s’approcha en tremblant & en admirant, & se mit à genoux auprés d’elle.
sentences.say: Il s’approcha en tremblant et en admirant, et se mit à genoux auprès d’elle.
sentences.l: He approached trembling and admiring, and put himself on his knees beside her.
sentences.i: He drew near, trembling and marvelling, and knelt down beside her.
sentences.n: «en tremblant & en admirant» are gerunds, ‘(while) trembling and admiring’, and «admirer» keeps its older force, ‘to gaze in wonder’. «se mettre à genoux» is ‘to kneel’, and «auprés» is the 1697 spelling of «auprès» ‘beside’.

sentences.t: Alors, comme la fin de l’enchantement estoit venuë, la Princesse s’éveilla ; & le regardant avec des yeux plus tendres qu’une premiere veuë ne sembloit le permettre ;
sentences.say: Alors, comme la fin de l’enchantement était venue, la Princesse s’éveilla ; et le regardant avec des yeux plus tendres qu’une première vue ne semblait le permettre ;
sentences.l: Then, as the end of the enchantment was come, the Princess awoke; and looking at him with eyes more tender than a first sight seemed to permit it;
sentences.i: Then, since the end of the enchantment had come, the Princess awoke, and looked at him with eyes more tender than a first meeting would seem to allow;
sentences.n: «estoit venuë» ‘was come’ is the pluperfect of «venir», formed with «estre», and «venuë» the 1697 spelling of «venue». After a comparison the «ne» in «ne sembloit le permettre» negates nothing, and «le» stands for the tender look itself. «veuë» (modern «vue») is ‘sight, seeing’: a first sight of someone ought not to allow such tenderness.

sentences.t: est ce vous, mon Prince, luy dit-elle ; vous vous estes bien fait attendre.
sentences.say: est ce vous, mon Prince, lui dit-elle ; vous vous êtes bien fait attendre.
sentences.l: is it you, my Prince, she said to him; you have indeed made yourself waited for.
sentences.i: Is it you, my Prince? she said. You have been a long time coming.
sentences.n: «se faire attendre» is ‘to keep others waiting’, literally ‘to make oneself be waited for’, and «bien» strengthens it; coming after a hundred years, the mild reproach is an understatement, whether or not the Princess means it as one. The witness prints «est ce» without its hyphen and with no question mark, and «estes» is the 1697 spelling of «êtes». «luy dit-elle» is ‘she said to him’, with «luy» for «lui».

sentences.t: Le Prince charmé de ces paroles, & plus encore de la maniere dont elles estoient dites, ne sçavoit comment luy témoigner sa joye & sa reconnoissance ; il l’assura qu’il l’aimoit plus que luy-mesme.
sentences.say: Le Prince charmé de ces paroles, et plus encore de la manière dont elles étaient dites, ne savait comment lui témoigner sa joie et sa reconnaissance ; il l’assura qu’il l’aimait plus que lui-même.
sentences.l: The Prince, charmed by these words, and more still by the manner in which they were said, knew not how to show her his joy and his gratitude; he assured her that he loved her more than himself.
sentences.i: The Prince, enchanted by these words, and still more by the way they were spoken, did not know how to show her his joy and gratitude; he assured her that he loved her more than himself.
sentences.n: «charmé» is stronger than modern ‘charmed’: ‘delighted, enraptured’, still close to «charme» ‘spell’, which is why the English says ‘enchanted’. «reconnoissance» (modern «reconnaissance») is ‘gratitude’ here, and «témoigner» ‘to show, give proof of’; «joye» is the 1697 spelling of «joie», and «ne sçavoit» is ‘did not know’ as before.

sentences.t: Ses discours furent mal rangez, ils en plurent davantage, peu d’éloquence, beaucoup d’amour :
sentences.l: His speeches were badly arranged, they pleased the more for it, little eloquence, much love:
sentences.i: His words came out in no good order, and were all the more pleasing for it: little eloquence, a great deal of love.
sentences.n: «plurent» is the passé simple of «plaire» ‘to please’, and «en» is ‘for it, on that account’: the disorder is the charm. «rangez» (modern «rangés») is ‘arranged, set in order’. The last two phrases have no verb, the narrator’s summing-up.

sentences.t: il estoit plus embarassé qu’elle, & l’on ne doit pas s’en estonner ;
sentences.say: il était plus embarrassé qu’elle, et l’on ne doit pas s’en étonner ;
sentences.l: he was more embarrassed than she, and one must not be astonished at it;
sentences.i: he was more at a loss than she was, and no one should wonder at it;
sentences.n: «embarassé» (modern «embarrassé») is ‘at a loss, awkward’ rather than ‘ashamed’. «l’on» is «on» with an «l’» added for the sound after «&», and «s’estonner» (modern «s’étonner») could carry more force in 1697 than now, ‘to be astounded’, though here it is simply ‘to wonder at’.

sentences.t: elle avoit eu le temps de songer à ce qu’elle auroit à luy dire, car il y a apparence (l’Histoire n’en dit pourtant rien) que la bonne fée pendant un si long sommeil, lui avoit procuré le plaisir des songes agreables.
sentences.say: elle avait eu le temps de songer à ce qu’elle aurait à lui dire, car il y a apparence (l’Histoire n’en dit pourtant rien) que la bonne fée pendant un si long sommeil, lui avait procuré le plaisir des songes agréables.
sentences.l: she had had the time to think about what she would have to say to him, for there is likelihood (the History however says nothing of it) that the good fairy, during so long a sleep, had procured her the pleasure of agreeable dreams.
sentences.i: she had had time to think over what she would say to him, for it seems likely (though the story says nothing of it) that during so long a sleep the good fairy had given her the pleasure of pleasant dreams.
sentences.n: «songer à» is ‘to think about’ and «songes» are ‘dreams’, two words from one root: she has had a hundred years of «songes» in which to «songer». «il y a apparence» is ‘it is likely’, and «l’Histoire» is ‘the story’: the narrator pretends to follow a written source that is silent on the point. «auroit» is «aurait» and «agreables» «agréables»; the witness prints both «luy» and «lui» in this one sentence.

sentences.t: Enfin il y avoit quatre heures qu’ils se parloient, & ils ne s’estoient pas encore dit la moitié des choses qu’ils avoient à se dire.
sentences.say: Enfin il y avait quatre heures qu’ils se parlaient, et ils ne s’étaient pas encore dit la moitié des choses qu’ils avaient à se dire.
sentences.l: In short, it had been four hours that they were speaking to each other, and they had not yet said to each other half of the things that they had to say to each other.
sentences.i: In short, they had been talking for four hours, and had not yet said half of what they had to say to each other.
sentences.n: «il y avoit quatre heures que» with the imperfect «parloient» is ‘they had been talking for four hours’: French keeps the imperfect for an action still going on. «se parler» and «se dire» are reciprocal, ‘to speak to each other’, ‘to say to each other’, and «Enfin» here sums up: ‘in short’.

sentences.t: Cependant tout le Palais s’estoit réveillé avec la Princesse : chacun songeoit à faire sa charge, & comme ils n’estoient pas tous amoureux, ils mouroient de faim.
sentences.say: Cependant tout le Palais s’était réveillé avec la Princesse : chacun songeait à faire sa charge, et comme ils n’étaient pas tous amoureux, ils mouraient de faim.
sentences.l: Meanwhile all the Palace had woken with the Princess: each one was thinking of doing his office, and as they were not all in love, they were dying of hunger.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the whole palace had woken with the Princess; everyone was thinking of getting on with his duties, and since they were not all in love, they were dying of hunger.
sentences.n: «Cependant» here keeps its older sense, ‘meanwhile’, not ‘however’. A «charge» is a post in a great household, and «faire sa charge» is ‘to do one’s office’. The joke is the narrator’s: lovers forget to eat, and servants who have gone a hundred years without a meal do not. «mouroient» is the 1697 spelling of «mouraient».

sentences.t: La Dame d’honneur, pressée comme les autres, s’impatienta, & dit tout haut à la Princesse que la viande estoit servie.
sentences.say: La Dame d’honneur, pressée comme les autres, s’impatienta, et dit tout haut à la Princesse que la viande était servie.
sentences.l: The Lady of honour, pressed like the others, grew impatient, and said out loud to the Princess that the food was served.
sentences.i: The lady of honour, as hard pressed as the rest, lost patience and announced aloud to the Princess that the meal was served.
sentences.n: The «Dame d’honneur» was the senior lady of a queen’s or princess’s household, first among her attendants. «viande», from a Latin word for ‘things to live on’, could still mean food of any kind, as it does in this announcement of the meal, though ‘meat’ was already becoming its usual sense. «pressée» is ‘hard pressed’, here by hunger, and «s’impatienta» is passé simple, ‘lost patience’.

sentences.t: Le Prince aida la princesse à se lever : elle estoit tout habillée, & fort magnifiquement ;
sentences.say: Le Prince aida la princesse à se lever : elle était tout habillée, et fort magnifiquement ;
sentences.l: The Prince helped the princess to get up: she was all dressed, and very magnificently;
sentences.i: The Prince helped the Princess to rise. She was fully dressed, and most magnificently;
sentences.n: «tout habillée» is ‘fully dressed’, «tout» here an adverb, ‘quite, entirely’: she has slept a hundred years in her day clothes. «fort» before an adjective or adverb is ‘very’, a use now old-fashioned. The witness prints «princesse» here without its usual capital.

sentences.t: mais il garda bien de luy dire qu’elle estoit habillée comme ma mere grand, & qu’elle avoit un collet monté, elle n’en estoit pas moins belle.
sentences.say: mais il garda bien de lui dire qu’elle était habillée comme ma mère grand, et qu’elle avait un collet monté, elle n’en était pas moins belle.
sentences.l: but he kept well from telling her that she was dressed like my grandmother, and that she had a stand-up collar; she was not the less beautiful for it.
