sentences.i: but he took good care not to tell her that she was dressed like my grandmother and wore a stiff high collar; she was none the less beautiful for it.
sentences.n: The idiom is «se garder de» ‘to take care not to’: the witness prints «il garda bien de» with no «se», which reads as a slip, whether the printer’s or the transcription’s, since the sense requires «il se garda bien de», and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. The text does not say whose «ma» it is in «ma mere grand» ‘my grandmother’ (modern «grand-mère»): the narrator may be breaking in, or the Prince’s unspoken words may be slipping into the reported speech; either way her clothes are a century out of date. The «collet monté» was a tall collar stiffened to stand up round the neck, the fashion of about a hundred years before; by Perrault’s day the phrase could also mean ‘stiff, prim, old-fashioned’.

sentences.t: Ils passerent dans un salon de miroirs, & y souperent, servis par les Officiers de la Princesse.
sentences.say: Ils passèrent dans un salon de miroirs, et y soupèrent, servis par les Officiers de la Princesse.
sentences.l: They passed into a salon of mirrors, and supped there, served by the Officers of the Princess.
sentences.i: They went through into a hall of mirrors and had supper there, waited on by the officers of the Princess’s household.
sentences.n: «souperent» (modern «soupèrent») is the passé simple of «souper», to take the evening meal. A room lined with mirrors was the height of luxury, and the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles had been finished little more than ten years before the book appeared. The «Officiers» are the officers of her household, the servants in charge of her table.

sentences.t: Les Violons & les Hautbois joüerent de vieilles pieces, mais excellentes, quoyqu’il y eut prés de cent ans qu’on ne les joüast plus ;
sentences.say: Les Violons et les Hautbois jouèrent de vieilles pièces, mais excellentes, quoiqu’il y eut prés de cent ans qu’on ne les jouât plus ;
sentences.l: The Violins and the Oboes played old pieces, but excellent ones, although it was nearly a hundred years that they were no longer played;
sentences.i: The violins and oboes played old pieces, but excellent ones, although no one had played them for nearly a hundred years;
sentences.n: «les Violons & les Hautbois» are the string and wind players of a court band; the King’s own string band was known as «les Vingt-quatre Violons du Roi». «quoyqu’il y eut» stands for «quoiqu’il y eût», subjunctive after «quoique» ‘although’, and «joüast» (modern «jouât») is imperfect subjunctive, with «ne … plus» ‘no longer’. «prés» is the 1697 spelling of «près» ‘near’, not modern «prés» ‘meadows’. The music, like the collar, is a hundred years out of date.

sentences.t: & aprés soupé, sans perdre de temps, le grand Aumonier les maria dans la Chapelle du Chasteau, & la Dame-d’honneur leur tira le rideau.
sentences.say: et après soupé, sans perdre de temps, le grand Aumônier les maria dans la Chapelle du Château, et la Dame-d’honneur leur tira le rideau.
sentences.l: and after supper, without losing any time, the grand Almoner married them in the Chapel of the Castle, and the Lady-of-honour drew the curtain on them.
sentences.i: and after supper, without wasting a moment, the Grand Almoner married them in the castle chapel, and the lady of honour drew the bed-curtain on them.
sentences.n: The «grand Aumonier» (modern «Grand Aumônier»), the Grand Almoner, was the senior churchman of a royal household. «aprés soupé» is ‘after supper’: «soupé» is the noun «souper» in a spelling the book uses again later («à son soupé»). «leur tira le rideau» is ‘drew the curtain on them’: the lady of honour closes the curtains of the bed on the newly married pair, the last duty of the wedding night.

sentences.t: Ils dormirent peu : la Princesse n’en avoit pas grand besoin, & le Prince la quitta dès le matin pour retourner à la Ville, où son pere devait estre en peine de luy :
sentences.say: Ils dormirent peu : la Princesse n’en avait pas grand besoin, et le Prince la quitta dès le matin pour retourner à la Ville, où son père devait être en peine de lui :
sentences.l: They slept little: the Princess had not great need of it, and the Prince left her from the morning to return to the City, where his father must be in trouble about him:
sentences.i: They slept little, for the Princess had no great need of sleep, and the Prince left her early in the morning to go back to the city, where his father was bound to be anxious about him;
sentences.n: «n’en avoit pas grand besoin» is ‘had no great need of it’: «en» is sleep, and after a hundred years she has had her fill. «dès le matin» is ‘first thing in the morning’. «devait estre en peine de luy» is ‘was bound to be worried about him’, with «devoir» of what is surely so; the witness prints «devait» here with the modern «-ait», where it usually has «-oit».

sentences.t: le Prince luy dit qu’en chassant il s’estait perdu dans la forest, & qu’il avait couché dans la hutte d’un Charbonnier, qui luy avoit fait manger du pain noir & du fromage.
sentences.say: le Prince lui dit qu’en chassant il s’était perdu dans la forêt, et qu’il avait couché dans la hutte d’un Charbonnier, qui lui avait fait manger du pain noir et du fromage.
sentences.l: the Prince told him that in hunting he had lost himself in the forest, and that he had slept in the hut of a Charcoal-burner, who had given him black bread and cheese to eat.
sentences.i: the Prince told him that he had lost his way in the forest while hunting and had spent the night in a charcoal-burner’s hut, where the man had fed him on black bread and cheese.
sentences.n: «luy» is the Prince’s father, and «il» the Prince. A «Charbonnier» burned wood into charcoal and lived in a rough hut deep in the forest; «pain noir», coarse dark bread, was the fare of the poor. «luy avoit fait manger» is literally ‘had made him eat’, «faire» with an infinitive, and «coucher» is ‘to spend the night’. «forest» is the 1697 spelling of «forêt», and «s’estait», «avait» mix the modern «-ait» into the 1697 spelling.

sentences.t: Le Roi son pere qui estoit bon-homme, le crut ;
sentences.say: Le Roi son père qui était bonhomme, le crut ;
sentences.l: The King his father, who was a good-natured man, believed him;
sentences.i: The King his father, a trusting soul, believed him;
sentences.n: «bon-homme» (modern «bonhomme») is a man of good nature and simple trust, easily taken in, and the word carries a touch of condescension. «crut» is the passé simple of «croire».

sentences.t: mais sa Mere n’en fut pas bien persuadée, & voyant qu’il alloit presque tous les jours à la chasse, & qu’il avoit toûjours une raison en main pour s’excuser quand il avoit couché deux ou trois nuits dehors, elle ne douta plus qu’il n’eut quelque amourette :
sentences.say: mais sa Mère n’en fut pas bien persuadée, et voyant qu’il allait presque tous les jours à la chasse, et qu’il avait toujours une raison en main pour s’excuser quand il avait couché deux ou trois nuits dehors, elle ne douta plus qu’il n’eut quelque amourette :
sentences.l: but his Mother was not well persuaded of it, and seeing that he went almost every day to the hunt, and that he always had a reason in hand to excuse himself when he had slept two or three nights out, she doubted no longer that he had some love-affair:
sentences.i: but his mother was not so easily convinced, and seeing that he went hunting almost every day, and always had an excuse ready whenever he had stayed away two or three nights, she no longer doubted that he had some love affair;
sentences.n: «amourette» is a passing love affair, a diminutive of «amour». After «ne douta plus que» the «ne» in «qu’il n’eut» negates nothing, and «eut» stands for the subjunctive «eût», printed without its circumflex. «une raison en main» ‘a reason in hand’ is an excuse ready to offer, and «alloit» is «allait».

sentences.t: car il vêcut avec la Princesse plus de deux ans entiers, & en eut deux enfans, dont le premier qui fut une fille, fut nommée l’Aurore, & le second un fils, qu’on nomma le Jour, parce qu’il paroissoit encore plus beau que sa sœur.
sentences.say: car il vécut avec la Princesse plus de deux ans entiers, et en eut deux enfants, dont le premier qui fut une fille, fut nommée l’Aurore, et le second un fils, qu’on nomma le Jour, parce qu’il paraissait encore plus beau que sa sœur.
sentences.l: for he lived with the Princess more than two whole years, and had of her two children, of whom the first, who was a daughter, was named Aurore, and the second a son, whom they named Jour, because he appeared even more beautiful than his sister.
sentences.i: for he lived with the Princess for more than two full years and had two children by her: the first, a daughter, was named Aurore, and the second, a son, was called Jour, because he seemed even more beautiful than his sister.
sentences.n: «l’Aurore» is ‘the Dawn’ and «le Jour» ‘the Day’; the names stay French in the English, and the boy outshines his sister as day outshines dawn. «le premier … fut nommée» begins masculine and ends feminine: the grammar follows the child, who turns out to be a girl. «vêcut» (modern «vécut») is the passé simple of «vivre», and in «en eut» the «en» stands for the Princess: ‘had of her’, that is, by her.

sentences.t: La Reine dit plusieurs fois à son fils, pour le faire expliquer, qu’il falloit se contenter dans la vie, mais il n’osa jamais se fier à elle de son secret ;
sentences.say: La Reine dit plusieurs fois à son fils, pour le faire expliquer, qu’il fallait se contenter dans la vie, mais il n’osa jamais se fier à elle de son secret ;
sentences.l: The Queen said several times to her son, to make him explain, that one must content oneself in life, but he never dared to trust her with his secret;
sentences.i: The Queen told her son more than once, to draw him out, that one should seek one’s contentment in life, but he never dared to trust her with his secret;
sentences.n: «pour le faire expliquer» ‘to make him explain’ leaves out the reflexive that modern French keeps, «pour le faire s’expliquer» ‘to make him explain himself’, as older French often did after «faire». Just what the Queen means by «il falloit se contenter dans la vie» is not certain: «se contenter» can be ‘to satisfy one’s wishes’, a hint that he may as well own to his love, or ‘to be content with what one has’; the English keeps it as open as it can. «se fier à quelqu’un de» is ‘to trust someone with’.

sentences.t: il la craignoit quoy qu’il l’aimast, car elle estoit de race Ogresse, & le Roi ne l’avoit épousée qu’à cause de ses grands biens.
sentences.say: il la craignait quoi qu’il l’aimât, car elle était de race Ogresse, et le Roi ne l’avait épousée qu’à cause de ses grands biens.
sentences.l: he feared her although he loved her, for she was of Ogress race, and the King had married her only because of her great wealth.
sentences.i: he was afraid of her although he loved her, for she came of Ogre stock, and the King had married her only for her great wealth.
sentences.n: «quoy qu’il l’aimast», modern «quoiqu’il l’aimât», has the imperfect subjunctive after ‘although’. «de race Ogresse» is ‘of Ogre blood’, with the feminine because it is the Queen who is of that race. «ne … qu’à cause de» is ‘only because of’, and «biens» are ‘possessions, wealth’: the old King married money.

sentences.t: On disoit même tout bas à la Cour qu’elle avoit les inclinations des Ogres, & qu’en voyant passer de petits enfans, elle avoit toutes les peines du monde à se retenir de se jeter sur eux ; ainsi le Prince ne voulut jamais rien dire.
sentences.say: On disait même tout bas à la Cour qu’elle avait les inclinations des Ogres, et qu’en voyant passer de petits enfants, elle avait toutes les peines du monde à se retenir de se jeter sur eux ; ainsi le Prince ne voulut jamais rien dire.
sentences.l: People said even very low at the Court that she had the inclinations of the Ogres, and that on seeing little children pass, she had all the trouble in the world to hold herself back from throwing herself on them; so the Prince would never say anything.
sentences.i: It was even whispered at court that she had the inclinations of the Ogres, and that when she saw little children go by, she could barely keep herself from falling upon them; and so the Prince would never say a word.
sentences.n: «tout bas» ‘all low’ is ‘in a whisper’, and «avoir toutes les peines du monde à» ‘to have all the trouble in the world to’ is to manage something only just. «inclinations» are natural leanings, here a taste for eating children. «ne voulut jamais rien dire» stacks «ne … jamais» and «rien», ‘never … anything’, as French does freely; «disoit» is «disait».

sentences.t: Mais, quand le Roy fut mort, ce qui arriva au bout de deux ans, & qu’il se vit le maistre, il declara publiquement son Mariage, & alla en grande ceremonie querir la Reine sa femme dans son Chasteau.
sentences.say: Mais, quand le Roi fut mort, ce qui arriva au bout de deux ans, et qu’il se vit le maître, il déclara publiquement son Mariage, et alla en grande cérémonie quérir la Reine sa femme dans son Château.
sentences.l: But, when the King was dead, which happened at the end of two years, and he saw himself the master, he declared publicly his Marriage, and went in great ceremony to fetch the Queen his wife in her Castle.
sentences.i: But when the King died, which happened two years later, and he found himself master, he made his marriage public and went in great state to fetch his wife the Queen from her castle.
sentences.n: The book spells the word both «Roy» and «Roi». «& qu’il se vit» takes up «quand» with «que», the French way of avoiding a second ‘when’. «querir» (modern «quérir») ‘to fetch’ survives only after verbs of going and sending. The Prince is now King, so «la Reine sa femme» is his wife, the new Queen.

sentences.t: On luy fit une entrée magnifique dans la Ville Capitale, où elle entra au milieu de ses deux enfans.
sentences.say: On lui fit une entrée magnifique dans la Ville Capitale, où elle entra au milieu de ses deux enfants.
sentences.l: They made for her a magnificent entry into the Capital City, where she entered in the middle of her two children.
sentences.i: She was given a magnificent entry into the capital, and came into it with her two children on either side of her.
sentences.n: An «entrée» was a formal ceremony: a king or queen coming to a city in state was met at the gates and led in procession through decorated streets. «au milieu de» ‘in the middle of’ puts her between the two children, and «On luy fit» is ‘they gave her’, with the impersonal «on».

sentences.t: Quelque temps aprés, le Roi alla faire la guerre à l’Empereur Cantalabutte, son voisin.
sentences.say: Quelque temps après, le Roi alla faire la guerre à l’Empereur Cantalabutte, son voisin.
sentences.l: Some time after, the King went to make war on the Emperor Cantalabutte, his neighbour.
sentences.i: Some time later, the King went off to make war on his neighbour, the Emperor Cantalabutte.
sentences.n: «Cantalabutte» is a comic-sounding name with no settled meaning, and it stays French. «le Roi» is now the former Prince, and «aprés» is the 1697 spelling of «après».

sentences.t: Il laissa la Regence du royaume à la Reine sa mere, & luy recommanda fort sa femme & ses enfans : il devoit estre à la guerre tout l’Esté ;
sentences.say: Il laissa la Régence du royaume à la Reine sa mère, et lui recommanda fort sa femme et ses enfants : il devait être à la guerre tout l’Été ;
sentences.l: He left the Regency of the kingdom to the Queen his mother, and commended strongly to her his wife and his children: he was to be at the war all the Summer;
sentences.i: He left the regency of the kingdom to his mother the Queen, and earnestly commended his wife and children to her care, for he was to be away at the war all summer;
sentences.n: The «Regence» is the rule of the kingdom in the king’s absence, and he leaves it to the Ogress. «recommander quelqu’un à» is ‘to commend someone to the care of’, and «fort» is ‘strongly, earnestly’. «Esté» is the 1697 spelling of «été» ‘summer’, and «devoit estre» is ‘was to be’.

sentences.t: et, dés qu’il fut parti, la Reine-Mere envoya sa bru & ses enfans à une maison de campagne dans les bois, pour pouvoir plus aisément assouvir son horrible envie.
sentences.say: et, dès qu’il fut parti, la Reine-mère envoya sa bru et ses enfants à une maison de campagne dans les bois, pour pouvoir plus aisément assouvir son horrible envie.
sentences.l: and, as soon as he was gone, the Queen-Mother sent her daughter-in-law and her children to a country house in the woods, to be able more easily to glut her horrible craving.
sentences.i: and as soon as he had gone, the Queen Mother sent her daughter-in-law and the children to a country house in the woods, so that she could more easily sate her horrible craving.
sentences.n: «la Reine-Mere» ‘the Queen Mother’ is the title of a reigning king’s mother. «bru» is ‘daughter-in-law’, and «ses enfans» are the young Queen’s children. «envie» is ‘craving, appetite’, and «assouvir» ‘to glut, sate’ is a word for hunger. The witness prints «et» here rather than its usual «&», and «fut parti» is ‘was gone’.

sentences.t: Elle y alla quelques jours aprés, & dit un soir à son Maistre d’Hostel, je veux manger demain à mon dîner la petite Aurore.
sentences.say: Elle y alla quelques jours après, et dit un soir à son Maître d’Hôtel, je veux manger demain à mon dîner la petite Aurore.
sentences.l: She went there some days after, and said one evening to her steward, I want to eat tomorrow at my dinner little Aurore.
sentences.i: She went there a few days later, and one evening said to her steward, I want to eat little Aurore for my dinner tomorrow.
sentences.n: The «Maistre d’Hostel» (modern «maître d’hôtel»), ‘the steward’, was the officer in charge of a great household’s table. The book sets speech down without quotation marks, joined to its speech tag by a comma, and the English does the same. The «dîner» was the midday meal and the «souper» the evening one.

sentences.t: Ah ! Madame, dit le Maistre-d’Hostel, je le veux, dit la Reine (& elle le dit d’un ton d’Ogresse qui a envie de manger de la chair fraische), & je la veux manger à la Sausse-robert.
sentences.say: Ah ! Madame, dit le Maître-d’Hôtel, je le veux, dit la Reine (et elle le dit d’un ton d’Ogresse qui a envie de manger de la chair fraîche), et je la veux manger à la Sauce-robert.
sentences.l: Ah! Madame, said the steward; I want it, said the Queen (and she said it in the tone of an Ogress who has a craving to eat fresh flesh), and I want to eat her with sauce Robert.
sentences.i: Ah! Madame, said the steward. I will have it so, said the Queen (and she said it in the voice of an Ogress who longs to eat fresh flesh), and I mean to eat her with sauce Robert.
sentences.n: Sauce Robert, printed «Sausse-robert» in 1697, is a real sauce of the French kitchen, made with onions and mustard and served above all with pork; English cookery keeps the French name, and so does the English here. «je la veux manger» sets the pronoun before «veux», the usual order in 1697, where modern French says «je veux la manger». The Ogress later wants the young Queen «à la mesme sausse» ‘with the same sauce’. «je le veux» ‘I will it’ cuts short the steward’s protest, and the witness runs his cry and her answer together with only commas, which the English breaks with a stop; «chair fraische» (modern «chair fraîche») is ‘fresh flesh’.

sentences.t: Ce pauvre homme, voyant bien qu’il ne falloit pas se joüer à une Ogresse, prit son grand cousteau, & monta à la chambre de la petite Aurore :
sentences.say: Ce pauvre homme, voyant bien qu’il ne fallait pas se jouer à une Ogresse, prit son grand couteau, et monta à la chambre de la petite Aurore :
sentences.l: This poor man, seeing well that one must not play with an Ogress, took his big knife, and went up to the room of little Aurore:
sentences.i: The poor man, seeing plainly that an Ogress was not to be trifled with, took his big knife and went up to little Aurore’s room.
sentences.n: «se joüer à» (modern «se jouer à») is ‘to trifle with’, and «il ne falloit pas» ‘one must not’. «cousteau» is the 1697 spelling of «couteau»; in the next sentence the witness prints «couteau», and both are the same knife.

sentences.t: elle avoit pour lors quatre ans, & vint en sautant & en riant se jetter à son col, & luy demander du bon bon.
sentences.say: elle avait pour lors quatre ans, et vint en sautant et en riant se jeter à son col, et lui demander du bon bon.
sentences.l: she was at that time four years old, and came leaping and laughing to throw herself on his neck, and to ask him for some good-good.
sentences.i: She was four years old at the time, and came skipping and laughing to throw her arms round his neck and ask him for sweets.
sentences.n: «bon bon», printed as two words, is a child’s doubling of «bon» ‘good’, the source of «bonbon» ‘sweet’. «col» is the older form of «cou» ‘neck’, and «se jetter à son col» ‘to throw herself at his neck’ is to hug him; «jetter» is «jeter». «pour lors» is ‘at that time’, and «avoir quatre ans» ‘to be four’.

sentences.t: Il se mit à pleurer, le couteau luy tomba des mains, & il alla dans la basse cour couper la gorge à un petit agneau, & luy fit une si bonne sausse que sa maistresse l’assura qu’elle n’avoit jamais rien mangé de si bon.
sentences.say: Il se mit à pleurer, le couteau lui tomba des mains, et il alla dans la basse cour couper la gorge à un petit agneau, et lui fit une si bonne sauce que sa maîtresse l’assura qu’elle n’avait jamais rien mangé de si bon.
sentences.l: He began to weep, the knife fell from his hands, and he went into the farmyard to cut the throat of a little lamb, and made for it so good a sauce that his mistress assured him that she had never eaten anything so good.
sentences.i: He burst into tears, the knife dropped from his hands, and he went down into the farmyard and cut the throat of a young lamb, and made so good a sauce for it that his mistress assured him she had never eaten anything so good.
sentences.n: «le couteau luy tomba des mains» ‘the knife fell to him from the hands’ has «luy» where English says ‘his’, the French way with parts of the body. «couper la gorge à» is ‘to cut the throat of’, and the «basse cour» (modern «basse-cour», as the witness prints it a sentence later) is the farmyard where poultry and small beasts were kept. In «luy fit une si bonne sausse», «luy» is most naturally the lamb, ‘made for it’, and «maistresse» is his mistress, the Queen Mother he serves.

sentences.t: Il avoit emporté en même temps la petite Aurore, & l’avoit donnée à sa femme, pour la cacher dans le logement qu’elle avoit au fond de la basse-cour.
sentences.say: Il avait emporté en même temps la petite Aurore, et l’avait donnée à sa femme, pour la cacher dans le logement qu’elle avait au fond de la basse-cour.
sentences.l: He had carried off at the same time little Aurore, and had given her to his wife, to hide her in the lodging that she had at the bottom of the farmyard.
sentences.i: At the same time he had carried little Aurore away and given her to his wife, to hide in the lodging she had at the far end of the farmyard.
sentences.n: The pluperfect «avoit emporté» steps back in time: this was done at the same time as the lamb. «au fond de» is ‘at the far end of’, out of the Queen’s sight. The witness prints «même» here with a circumflex, where it often has «mesme».

sentences.t: Huit jours après, la méchante Reine dit à son Maistre-d’Hostel, je veux manger à mon souper le petit Jour : il ne répliqua pas, résolu de la tromper comme l’autre fois ;
sentences.say: Huit jours après, la méchante Reine dit à son Maître-d’Hôtel, je veux manger à mon souper le petit Jour : il ne répliqua pas, résolu de la tromper comme l’autre fois ;
sentences.l: Eight days after, the wicked Queen said to her steward, I want to eat at my supper little Jour: he did not reply, resolved to deceive her as the other time;
sentences.i: A week later the wicked Queen said to her steward, I want to eat little Jour for my supper. He made no reply, having made up his mind to deceive her as he had before;
sentences.n: «Huit jours» ‘eight days’ is the French for ‘a week’, counting both ends. «le petit Jour» is ‘little Jour’, though «le petit jour» is also French for the first light of morning, and the name may play on it. «répliqua» is passé simple, ‘answered back’, and «résolu de» is ‘resolved to’.

sentences.t: il alla chercher le petit Jour, & le trouva avec un petit fleuret à la main, dont il faisoit des armes avec un gros Singe : il n’avoit pourtant que trois ans.
sentences.say: il alla chercher le petit Jour, et le trouva avec un petit fleuret à la main, dont il faisait des armes avec un gros Singe : il n’avait pourtant que trois ans.
sentences.l: he went to fetch little Jour, and found him with a little foil in his hand, with which he was fencing with a big Monkey: he was, however, only three years old.
sentences.i: he went to look for little Jour, and found him with a little foil in his hand, fencing with a big monkey, though he was only three years old.
sentences.n: A «fleuret» is a foil, the light sword with a button on its point used for fencing bouts, and «faire des armes» is ‘to fence’. A great house might keep a monkey as a pet. «ne … que» is ‘only’ again, and «alla chercher» is ‘went to fetch’.

sentences.t: Il le porta à sa femme, qui le cacha avec la petite Aurore, & donna à la place du petit Jour, un petit chevreau fort tendre, que l’Ogresse trouva admirablement bon.
sentences.say: Il le porta à sa femme, qui le cacha avec la petite Aurore, et donna à la place du petit Jour, un petit chevreau fort tendre, que l’Ogresse trouva admirablement bon.
sentences.l: He carried him to his wife, who hid him with little Aurore, and [he] gave, in the place of little Jour, a very tender little kid, which the Ogress found admirably good.
sentences.i: He carried him to his wife, who hid him with little Aurore, and in little Jour’s place [he] served a very tender young kid, which the Ogress found wonderfully good.
sentences.n: The French leaves the subject of «donna» unstated, so that grammatically it could be the wife; the sense is that the steward gave the kid to the Queen, and the English supplies ‘he’ in brackets. A «chevreau» is a young goat, and «fort tendre» is ‘very tender’. «admirablement» is ‘wonderfully’, «admirer» still carrying its sense of wonder.

sentences.t: Cela estoit fort bien allé jusque là, mais un soir cette méchante reine dit au Maistre-d’Hostel, je veux manger la Reine à la mesme sausse que ses enfans.
sentences.say: Cela était fort bien allé jusque là, mais un soir cette méchante reine dit au Maître-d’Hôtel, je veux manger la Reine à la même sauce que ses enfants.
sentences.l: That had gone very well up to then, but one evening this wicked Queen said to the steward, I want to eat the Queen with the same sauce as her children.
sentences.i: All had gone very well so far, but one evening the wicked Queen said to the steward: I want to eat the young Queen with the same sauce as her children.
sentences.n: «estoit allé» is ‘had gone’: «aller» forms its compound tenses with «estre», so the imperfect of «estre» with «allé» makes a pluperfect; «jusque là» is modern «jusque-là» ‘up to then’. The wicked queen is the Queen Mother, and the «Reine» she wants to eat is her son’s wife, the young Queen, as the idiomatic line makes plain; the witness prints the title with a capital or without, as it does throughout. «à la mesme sausse» ‘with the same sauce’ is the sauce Robert she ordered for little Aurore («mesme», «sausse» and «enfans» are 1697 spellings of «même», «sauce», «enfants»). As before, her words are set off by a comma alone, with no quotation marks.

sentences.t: Ce fut alors que le pauvre Maistre-d’Hostel desespera de la pouvoir encore tromper.
sentences.say: Ce fut alors que le pauvre Maître-d’Hôtel désespéra de la pouvoir encore tromper.
sentences.l: It was then that the poor steward despaired of being able to deceive her again.
sentences.i: It was then that the poor steward gave up hope of deceiving her any longer.
sentences.n: «Ce fut alors que» is ‘it was then that’, with «fut», the passé simple of «estre». «la pouvoir encore tromper» sets the pronoun «la» ‘her’ before «pouvoir», the usual 1697 order, where modern French says «pouvoir encore la tromper». «desespera» is modern «désespéra», without the accents.

sentences.t: La jeune reine avoit vingt ans passez, sans compter les cent ans qu’elle avoit dormi :
sentences.say: La jeune reine avait vingt ans passez, sans compter les cent ans qu’elle avait dormi :
sentences.l: The young Queen had twenty years passed, without counting the hundred years that she had slept:
sentences.i: The young Queen was past twenty, not counting the hundred years she had slept:
sentences.n: French gives age with «avoir», ‘to have’ so many years, and «vingt ans passez» is ‘twenty years passed’, that is, over twenty; «passez» is the 1697 spelling of «passés». The hundred years asleep are the narrator’s dry aside, and they lead into the remark about her skin that follows.

sentences.t: sa peau estoit un peu dure, quoyque belle & blanche ; & le moyen de trouver dans la Menagerie une beste aussi dure que cela :
sentences.say: sa peau était un peu dure, quoique belle et blanche ; et le moyen de trouver dans la Ménagerie une bête aussi dure que cela :
sentences.l: her skin was a little tough, although beautiful and white; and the means of finding in the Menagerie a beast as tough as that:
sentences.i: her skin was a little tough, fair and white though it was; and how was he to find a beast in the menagerie as tough as that?
sentences.n: «dure» is ‘hard, tough’, the word for tough meat: the young Queen is being weighed up as a dish. «le moyen de» with an infinitive is an exclamation of impossibility, ‘what way was there to …’, and the witness closes it with a colon, not a question mark. A «Menagerie» (modern «ménagerie») in Perrault’s day was a farmstead where livestock and poultry were kept and fattened for a great house, and also the name of the King’s collection of rare animals at Versailles; here it is most likely the household’s yard of animals. «quoyque» and «beste» are 1697 spellings of «quoique» and «bête».

sentences.t: il prit la resolution, pour sauver sa vie, de couper la gorge à la reine, & monta dans sa chambre, dans l’intention de n’en pas faire à deux fois ;
sentences.say: il prit la résolution, pour sauver sa vie, de couper la gorge à la reine, et monta dans sa chambre, dans l’intention de n’en pas faire à deux fois ;
sentences.l: he took the resolution, to save his life, of cutting the Queen’s throat, and went up into her room, with the intention of not making two goes of it;
sentences.i: To save his own life he resolved to cut the Queen’s throat, and he went up to her room meaning to do it at a single stroke;
sentences.n: «couper la gorge à la reine» is ‘to cut the throat to the queen’: French names the one whose body it is with «à», as it did for the lamb, where English says ‘the Queen’s throat’. «n’en pas faire à deux fois» ‘not to make two times of it’ means to do a thing in one go, without faltering. «sa chambre» here is her room, the young Queen’s; «resolution» is modern «résolution».

sentences.t: il s’excitoit à la fureur, & entra le poignard à la main dans la chambre de la jeune Reine :
sentences.say: il s’excitait à la fureur, et entra le poignard à la main dans la chambre de la jeune Reine :
sentences.l: he was stirring himself to fury, and went, the dagger in his hand, into the room of the young Queen:
sentences.i: he worked himself up into a fury and went into the young Queen’s room, dagger in hand;
sentences.n: «s’excitoit» is the imperfect of «s’exciter» ‘to rouse oneself’: the imperfect shows him working himself up as he goes, and the passé simple «entra» ‘went in’ is the single act. «le poignard à la main» is ‘the dagger in the hand’, the French way of saying ‘dagger in hand’.

sentences.t: il ne voulut pourtant point la surprendre, & il luy dit avec beaucoup de respect, l’ordre qu’il avoit receu de la Reine-Mere.
sentences.say: il ne voulut pourtant point la surprendre, et il lui dit avec beaucoup de respect, l’ordre qu’il avait reçu de la Reine-mère.
sentences.l: he did not wish, however, to surprise her, and he told her with much respect the order that he had received from the Queen Mother.
sentences.i: yet he would not take her unawares, and with great respect he told her the order he had received from the Queen Mother.
sentences.n: «ne … point» is a stronger ‘not’. «surprendre» here is ‘to take unawares’, to fall on her before she knows. «receu» is the 1697 spelling of «reçu» ‘received’, and the comma before «l’ordre», which parts the verb from its object, is the witness’s.

sentences.t: Faites, faites, luy dit-elle en luy tendant le col ; executez l’ordre qu’on vous a donné ; j’irai revoir mes enfans, mes pauvres enfans, que j’ay tant aimez :
sentences.say: Faites, faites, lui dit-elle en lui tendant le col ; exécutez l’ordre qu’on vous a donné ; j’irai revoir mes enfants, mes pauvres enfants, que j’ai tant aimez :
sentences.l: Do, do, she said to him, holding out to him the neck; carry out the order that one has given you; I shall go to see again my children, my poor children, whom I have so loved:
sentences.i: Do it, do it, she said, holding out her neck to him; carry out the order you have been given. I shall go and see my children again, my poor children, whom I loved so dearly.
sentences.n: «Faites» is the imperative of «faire», used on its own: ‘do (it)’. In «tendant le col» ‘holding out the neck’, «col» is the older form of «cou» ‘neck’, and French says «le» where English says ‘her’. «j’irai revoir mes enfans» ‘I shall go to see my children again’ means in death, for she thinks them dead. «executez» is modern «exécutez», and «aimez» the 1697 spelling of «aimés», agreeing with «enfans».

sentences.t: elle les croyoit morts depuis qu’on les avoit enlevez sans luy rien dire.
sentences.say: elle les croyait morts depuis qu’on les avait enlevés sans lui rien dire.
sentences.l: she believed them dead since one had carried them off without telling her anything.
sentences.i: She had believed them dead ever since they were carried off without a word to her.
sentences.n: «on les avoit enlevez» ‘one had carried them off’: French uses «on» ‘one, someone’ where English prefers a passive, ‘they had been taken away’. «sans luy rien dire» sets both «luy» ‘to her’ and «rien» ‘anything’ before the infinitive. «croyoit» and «enlevez» are 1697 spellings of «croyait» and «enlevés».

sentences.t: Non, non, Madame, lui répondit le pauvre Maistre d’Hostel tout attendri, vous ne mourrez point, & vous ne laisserez pas d’aller revoir vos chers enfans ;
sentences.say: Non, non, Madame, lui répondit le pauvre Maître d’Hôtel tout attendri, vous ne mourrez point, et vous ne laisserez pas d’aller revoir vos chers enfants ;
sentences.l: No, no, Madame, the poor steward answered her, all softened, you will not die, and you will not fail to go and see your dear children again;
sentences.i: No, no, Madame, answered the poor steward, deeply moved, you shall not die, and you shall see your dear children again all the same;
sentences.n: «vous ne laisserez pas d’aller» uses «ne pas laisser de» ‘not to fail to’, met earlier in the tale, which means ‘all the same, nonetheless’: she will see her children, only not in the way she means. «tout attendri» is ‘quite softened, moved to pity’, and «mourrez» the future of «mourir» ‘to die’. The witness prints «Maistre d’Hostel» here without its hyphen, and «lui» with an i beside «luy» elsewhere.

sentences.t: mais ce sera chez moy où je les ay cachez, & je tromperay encore la Reine, en luy faisant manger une jeune biche en vostre place.
sentences.say: mais ce sera chez moi où je les ai cachés, et je tromperai encore la Reine, en lui faisant manger une jeune biche en votre place.
sentences.l: but it will be at my house where I have hidden them, and I shall deceive the Queen again, by making her eat a young doe in your place.
sentences.i: but it will be in my own lodging, where I have hidden them, and I shall deceive the Queen once more by giving her a young doe to eat in your stead.
sentences.n: «ce sera chez moy où» ‘it will be at my house where’ uses «où» where modern French would say «que» (‘it is at my house that’). «la Reine» is the Queen Mother now. «luy faisant manger» ‘making her eat’ is «faire» with an infinitive, and a «biche» is a doe, a female deer. «moy», «ay», «cachez», «tromperay» and «vostre» are 1697 spellings of «moi», «ai», «cachés», «tromperai» and «votre».

sentences.t: Il la mena aussi-tost à sa chambre, où la laissant embrasser ses enfans & pleurer avec eux : il alla accommoder une biche, que la reine mangea à son soupé, avec le même appetit que si c’eut esté la jeune reine.
sentences.say: Il la mena aussitôt à sa chambre, où la laissant embrasser ses enfants et pleurer avec eux : il alla accommoder une biche, que la reine mangea à son soupé, avec le même appétit que si c’eut été la jeune reine.
sentences.l: He led her at once to his room, where, leaving her to embrace her children and weep with them, he went to prepare a doe, which the Queen ate at her supper, with the same appetite as if it had been the young Queen.
sentences.i: He took her straight to his own quarters and there, leaving her to embrace her children and weep with them, he went and dressed a doe, which the Queen Mother ate at supper with as much appetite as if it had been the young Queen.
sentences.n: «sa chambre» could be ‘her room’ or ‘his’; the sense is his, the lodging where his wife keeps the children hidden. The witness sets a colon in the middle of the sentence, after «pleurer avec eux», and the English reads straight through it. «accommoder» is a kitchen word here, ‘to prepare, dress (meat)’, and «soupé» is «souper», the evening meal. «c’eut esté» is the pluperfect subjunctive, ‘it had been’, after «que si» ‘as if’, a literary turn where everyday French says «c’avait été»; the witness prints «eut» without the circumflex of «eût», so the form looks like the passé antérieur, but the sense requires the subjunctive. «aussi-tost» is modern «aussitôt» ‘at once’.

sentences.t: Elle estoit bien contente de sa cruauté, & elle se préparoit à dire au Roi à son retour, que des loups enragez avoient mangez la Reine sa femme & ses deux enfans.
sentences.say: Elle était bien contente de sa cruauté, et elle se préparait à dire au Roi à son retour, que des loups enragés avaient mangez la Reine sa femme et ses deux enfants.
sentences.l: She was well content with her cruelty, and she was preparing to tell the King on his return that some rabid wolves had eaten the Queen his wife and his two children.
sentences.i: She was well pleased with her cruelty, and was making ready to tell the King, when he came back, that rabid wolves had eaten the Queen his wife and his two children.
sentences.n: «loups enragez» are ‘rabid wolves’: «enragé», from «rage» ‘rabies’, is still the word for a mad dog. «avoient mangez» makes the participle agree with the plural object that follows it, which modern French would not do («avaient mangé»); usage in 1697 was less settled. «sa femme» and «ses deux enfans» are the King’s: ‘his wife’, ‘his two children’.

sentences.t: Un soir qu’elle rodoit à son ordinaire, dans les cours & basses-cours du chasteau pour y halener quelque viande fraische, elle entendit dans une salle basse le petit Jour qui pleuroit, parce que la Reine sa mere le vouloit faire foüetter, à cause qu’il avoit esté méchant,
sentences.say: Un soir qu’elle rôdait à son ordinaire, dans les cours et basses-cours du château pour y halener quelque viande fraîche, elle entendit dans une salle basse le petit Jour qui pleurait, parce que la Reine sa mère le voulait faire fouetter, à cause qu’il avait été méchant,
sentences.l: One evening that she was prowling as was her habit, in the courtyards and farmyards of the castle to scent out there some fresh meat, she heard in a low room little Jour who was crying, because the Queen his mother wanted to have him whipped, because he had been naughty,
sentences.i: One evening, while she was prowling as usual about the courtyards and farmyards of the castle, nosing for fresh meat, she heard little Jour crying in a ground-floor room, because the Queen his mother meant to have him whipped for being naughty,
sentences.n: «qu’» after «un soir» is ‘when’. «rodoit» (modern «rôdait») is ‘was prowling’, and «à son ordinaire» ‘as was her habit’. The «chasteau» is the country house in the woods to which she had sent the young Queen and the children; «chasteau» (modern «château») covered any great country seat, and ‘castle’ should not suggest the Princess’s own. «halener» is a hunting word, ‘to catch the scent of’, as a hound does, built on «haleine» ‘breath’. «viande» in 1697 could still mean food of any kind, as when the Princess was told the meal was served, but to an Ogress’s nose «viande fraische» is fresh flesh. A «salle basse» is a room on the ground floor. «le vouloit faire foüetter» ‘wanted to have him whipped’ is «faire» with an infinitive, the pronoun set before «vouloit», and «à cause qu’» is an older conjunction for «parce que» ‘because’; «méchant» of a small child is ‘naughty’, the same word that makes the Ogress ‘wicked’. «Jour» is ‘Day’.

sentences.t: & elle entendit aussi la petite Aurore qui demandoit pardon pour son frere.
sentences.say: et elle entendit aussi la petite Aurore qui demandait pardon pour son frère.
sentences.l: and she heard also little Aurore who was asking pardon for her brother.
sentences.i: and she heard little Aurore too, begging forgiveness for her brother.
sentences.n: After a verb of hearing or seeing, French uses «qui» and a verb, ‘Aurore who was asking’, where English says ‘Aurore asking’. «la petite Aurore» has the article because of the adjective, as French puts one before any name with an adjective (and the girl was named «l’Aurore», ‘the Dawn’, article and all); English says simply ‘little Aurore’. «demandoit pardon» is ‘begged forgiveness’; «frere» is modern «frère».

sentences.t: L’Ogresse reconnut la voix de la Reine & de ses enfans,
sentences.say: L’Ogresse reconnut la voix de la Reine et de ses enfants,
sentences.l: The Ogress recognised the voice of the Queen and of her children,
sentences.i: The Ogress knew the voices of the Queen and her children,
sentences.n: «reconnut» is the passé simple of «reconnoistre» (modern «reconnaître») ‘to recognise’. French says «la voix», in the singular, for the voice of each of them, where English says ‘voices’.

sentences.t: et, furieuse d’avoir esté trompée, elle commande, dés le lendemain matin, avec une voix épouvantable, qui faisoit trembler tout le monde, qu’on apportast au milieu de la cour une grande cuve, qu’elle fit remplir de crapaux, de viperes, de couleuvres & de serpens, pour y faire jetter la Reine & ses enfans, le Maistre d’Hostel, sa femme & sa servante ;
sentences.say: et, furieuse d’avoir été trompée, elle commande, dès le lendemain matin, avec une voix épouvantable, qui faisait trembler tout le monde, qu’on apportât au milieu de la cour une grande cuve, qu’elle fit remplir de crapauds, de vipères, de couleuvres et de serpents, pour y faire jeter la Reine et ses enfants, le Maître d’Hôtel, sa femme et sa servante ;
sentences.l: and, furious at having been deceived, she orders, first thing the next morning, with a dreadful voice, which made everyone tremble, that one should bring into the middle of the courtyard a great vat, which she had filled with toads, with vipers, with grass snakes and with serpents, in order to have thrown into it the Queen and her children, the steward, his wife and his maidservant;
sentences.i: and, furious at having been deceived, first thing the next morning she ordered, in a dreadful voice that set everyone trembling, a great vat to be brought into the middle of the courtyard and filled with toads, vipers, grass snakes and serpents, so that the Queen and her children, the steward, his wife and his maidservant might be thrown into it;
sentences.n: «commande» is in the present tense, a sudden switch from the passé simple around it that sets the order before the reader’s eyes; the idiomatic line keeps to the past. «qu’on apportast» ‘that one should bring’ is the imperfect subjunctive (modern «apportât») after a verb of ordering; the imperfect, where the present «commande» would lead one to expect the present subjunctive «apporte», shows that the telling is still thought of as past. «dés le lendemain matin» is ‘as early as the next morning’ («dés» for «dès»). «couleuvres» are grass snakes and their kin, harmless, as distinct from the venomous «viperes»; «crapaux» and «serpens» are 1697 spellings of «crapauds» and «serpents». «qu’elle fit remplir» and «y faire jetter» are both «faire» with an infinitive, ‘had filled’ and ‘have thrown’; «sa servante» is the maidservant of the steward’s household.

sentences.t: elle avoit donné ordre de les amener les mains liées derriere le dos.
sentences.say: elle avait donné ordre de les amener les mains liées derrière le dos.
sentences.l: she had given order to bring them with the hands tied behind the back.
sentences.i: she had given orders that they be brought with their hands tied behind their backs.
sentences.n: The pluperfect «avoit donné» ‘had given’ shows the order already given. In «les mains liées» ‘the hands tied’, an absolute phrase, French again says «les» and «le» where English says ‘their’. «derriere» is modern «derrière».

sentences.t: Ils estoient là, & les bourreaux se preparoient à les jetter dans la cuve, lorsque le Roi qu’on n’attendoit pas sitost, entra dans la cour, à cheval ;
sentences.say: Ils étaient là, et les bourreaux se préparaient à les jeter dans la cuve, lorsque le Roi qu’on n’attendait pas sitôt, entra dans la cour, à cheval ;
sentences.l: They were there, and the executioners were preparing to throw them into the vat, when the King, whom one was not expecting so soon, entered into the courtyard, on horseback;
sentences.i: There they stood, and the executioners were making ready to throw them into the vat, when the King, who was not expected so soon, rode into the courtyard;
sentences.n: The imperfects «estoient» and «se preparoient» hold the scene still, and the passé simple «entra» breaks in on it. «bourreaux» are executioners, the officers who carried out sentences of death. «sitost» is modern «sitôt» ‘so soon’, and «jetter» modern «jeter».

sentences.t: il estoit venu en poste & demanda tout estonné ce que vouloit dire cet horrible spectacle.
sentences.say: il était venu en poste et demanda tout étonné ce que voulait dire cet horrible spectacle.
sentences.l: he had come by post and asked, all astonished, what this horrible spectacle meant.
sentences.i: he had ridden post-haste, and he asked in astonishment what this horrible sight might mean.
sentences.n: To come «en poste» was to travel with post horses, changing to fresh mounts at the relay stations along the road, the fastest way to cover a long distance. «estonné» (modern «étonné») could still carry more force in 1697 than today: ‘thunderstruck’ rather than merely ‘surprised’. «ce que vouloit dire» sets the subject after its verb, and «vouloir dire» is ‘to mean’.

sentences.t: Personne n’osoit l’en instruire, quand l’Ogresse, enragée de voir ce qu’elle voyoit, se jeta elle-mesme la teste la premiere dans la cuve, & fut devorée en un instant par les vilaines bestes qu’elle y avoit fait mettre.
sentences.say: Personne n’osait l’en instruire, quand l’Ogresse, enragée de voir ce qu’elle voyait, se jeta elle-même la tête la première dans la cuve, et fut dévorée en un instant par les vilaines bêtes qu’elle y avait fait mettre.
sentences.l: No one dared to inform him of it, when the Ogress, enraged to see what she was seeing, threw herself head first into the vat, and was devoured in an instant by the foul beasts that she had had put in it.
sentences.i: No one dared tell him, when the Ogress, maddened at the sight before her, flung herself head first into the vat and was devoured in an instant by the vile creatures she had had put there.
sentences.n: «n’osoit l’en instruire» is ‘dared not inform him of it’, with «en» ‘of it’. «enragée», the word her lie used for the ‘rabid’ wolves, here means ‘maddened, beside herself’. «elle-mesme» ‘herself’ stresses that she does it by her own act, and «la teste la premiere» is ‘head first’. «vilaines bestes» are ‘foul beasts’: «vilain» meant base or ugly, more than today’s ‘nasty’.

sentences.t: Le roi ne laissa pas d’en estre fasché, elle estoit sa mere, mais il s’en consola bientost avec sa belle femme & ses enfans.
sentences.say: Le roi ne laissa pas d’en être fâché, elle était sa mère, mais il s’en consola bientôt avec sa belle femme et ses enfants.
sentences.l: The King did not fail to be grieved by it, she was his mother, but he consoled himself for it soon with his beautiful wife and his children.
sentences.i: The King was grieved by it all the same, for she was his mother, but he soon found consolation in his beautiful wife and his children.
sentences.n: «ne laissa pas d’en estre fasché» is «ne pas laisser de» once more, ‘did not fail to be grieved’, that is, he was grieved all the same. «fasché» (modern «fâché») meant ‘distressed, sorry’ in 1697, the sense of the tale’s first sentence, where the King and Queen are «si faschez» at having no children, not ‘angry’. The idiomatic line supplies ‘for’ where the French simply sets «elle estoit sa mere» between commas.

sentences.t: MORALITÉ
sentences.l: MORAL
sentences.n: «MORALITÉ» is ‘moral’: the verses that follow belong to the tale as Perrault printed it, for each tale in the book closes with a moral in verse.

sentences.t:
Attendre quelque temps pour avoir un Époux
Riche, bien-fait, galant & doux,
La chose est assez naturelle :
sentences.say:
Attendre quelque temps pour avoir un Époux,
Riche, bien-fait, galant et doux,
La chose est assez naturelle :
sentences.l:
To wait some time to have a husband
Rich, well-made, gallant and gentle,
The thing is natural enough:
sentences.n: The infinitive «Attendre» ‘to wait’ opens the sentence as its topic, and «La chose» ‘the thing’ picks it up: ‘waiting …, that is natural enough’. «bien-fait» is ‘well made’, handsome in face and figure. «galant» in 1697 meant polished and pleasing in society, attentive above all to women; English ‘gallant’, which leans toward ‘brave’, is only a near match, so the idiomatic line says ‘courtly’. «Époux» is ‘husband, spouse’.

sentences.t:
Mais l’attendre cent ans, & toûjours en dormant,
On ne trouve plus de femelle
Qui dormist si tranquillement.
sentences.say:
Mais l’attendre cent ans, et toujours en dormant,
On ne trouve plus de femelle,
Qui dormît si tranquillement.
sentences.l:
But to wait for him a hundred years, and all the while sleeping,
One finds no more a female
Who would sleep so tranquilly.
sentences.i:
But to wait a hundred years for him, and asleep the whole time,
You will find no woman nowadays
Who would sleep so calmly.
sentences.n: «l’attendre» is ‘to wait for him’, the husband: «attendre» takes a direct object, so French needs no ‘for’. This time the infinitive at the head of the sentence is never taken up again. «femelle» ‘female’, a word for animals, is applied to women in jest. «dormist» (modern «dormît») is the imperfect subjunctive, in a relative clause after a negative; «toûjours» is the 1697 spelling of «toujours».

sentences.t:
La Fable semble encor vouloir nous faire entendre
Que souvent de l’Hymen les agreables nœuds,
Pour estre differez, n’en sont pas moins heureux,
Et qu’on ne perd rien pour attendre.
sentences.say:
La Fable semble encor vouloir nous faire entendre,
Que souvent de l’Hymen les agréables nœuds,
Pour être différés, n’en sont pas moins heureux,
Et qu’on ne perd rien pour attendre.
sentences.l:
The Fable seems besides to want to make us understand
That often of Hymen the pleasant knots,
For being deferred, are not the less happy for it,
And that one loses nothing for waiting.
sentences.i:
The fable also seems to want to tell us
That the pleasant bonds of marriage are often
No less happy for being put off,
And that nothing is lost by waiting.
sentences.n: «encor» is a verse spelling of «encore», here ‘also, besides’, and «faire entendre» is ‘to give to understand’. «Hymen», the god of marriage in Greek and Roman poetry, stands for marriage itself, and the line sets «de l’Hymen» before the noun it belongs to: ‘the pleasant knots of Hymen’. «Pour estre differez» ‘for being deferred’ means ‘for all that they are put off’, and «n’en sont pas moins» is ‘are none the less for it’. The last line is a proverb, ‘one loses nothing by waiting’.

sentences.t:
Mais le sexe avec tant d’ardeur
Aspire à la foy conjugale
Que je n’ay pas la force ny le cœur
De luy prescher cette morale.
sentences.say:
Mais le sexe avec tant d’ardeur,
Aspire à la foi conjugale,
Que je n’ai pas la force ni le cœur,
De lui prêcher cette morale.
sentences.l:
But the sex with so much ardour
Aspires to the conjugal faith
That I have not the strength nor the heart
To preach to it this moral.
sentences.i:
But women long so ardently
For the marriage bond
That I have neither the strength nor the heart
To preach this moral to them.
sentences.n: «le sexe», used on its own in the French of the period, meant women, as English once said ‘the sex’ or ‘the fair sex’; «luy» ‘to it’ therefore means ‘to them’. «la foy conjugale» ‘conjugal faith’ is the pledge of marriage, and «tant … que» is ‘so much … that’. «foy», «ny», «n’ay» and «prescher» are 1697 spellings of «foi», «ni», «n’ai» and «prêcher». The poet ends by teasing women for an eagerness to marry that he claims not to have the heart to reprove.
